(for-statement)=

# The `for` Statement



```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```


The `for` statement executes a statement or a block of statements
while a specified **Boolean expression** evaluates to true. Such evaluation involves
comparing the local loop counter variable (an **integer counter** that increments/decrements over every loop)
to a preset value. Since the number of loops is controlled by comparing the counter with the **preset value**,
you need to specify the preset value to decide the number of times you want to run the code block when defining
a `for` loop statement.

(for-loop-header)=



```{index} For Statement Syntax
```



```{index} For Statement Syntax
```

## For Statement Syntax




`for` loops are usually favored for iteration because the
all the information about the local loop variable are available in one place at the top,
which helps quickly visualize the overall sequence in the loop.

The C# for loop statement syntax is:

```csharp
for ( *initializer* ; *condition* ; *iterator* )
{
// code block (statements)
}
```

Let us practice with `csharprepl`, `Run C#`, or a small VS Code project:


for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++)
{
      Console.WriteLine(i);
}

You can see that the `for` loop has four parts, a three-section semicolon-separated **header**
and a **body**:

- **Initializer**: This section is a **variable declaration statement** that
  declares a `local loop variable` (or `iterator variable` or the counter) and initialize it with an initial value.
- **Condition**: The condition section is a **boolean expression** that determines
  if the next iteration in the loop should be executed or should the loop be terminated. If it evaluates to true,
  the next iteration is executed; otherwise, the loop is exited.
- **Iterator**: The iterator (**iteration expression**) section that defines what happens to the counter after each
  execution of the body of the loop. A common behavior is reassigning
  (increment or decrement) the value of the counter.
- The **body** of the loop, which must be a statement or a block of statements.

In the example above, the *initializer* is `i = 1`, *condition* is `i <= n`,
and *iterator* is `i++` (see {ref}`arithmetic operators <arithmetic-operators>`).

Note that the initializer section is executed **only once**, before entering the loop.
Also, the declared variable is local to the `for` loop heading and
the loop body and can not be accessed from outside the for statement.

The two semicolons are always needed in the `for` heading, but any of the
parts they normally separate may be omitted.
If the condition part is omitted, the condition is
interpreted as always true, leading to an infinite loop, that can only
terminate due to a `return` or {ref}`break statement <break-continue>` in the body.

**Header variation**

The declaration of a for loop header is flexible. There may be several variables of the
same type initialized, separated by commas. Also, at the end of the `for` loop heading,
the iteration portion may include more than one expression, also separated by commas.
For example:

for (int i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i = i+2, j++) {
   Console.WriteLine("{0} {1}", i, j);
}


Guess what this does, and then run it with `csharprepl`, `Run C#`, or a small VS Code project to check.


```{index} execution sequence; for loop
```



```{index} Execution sequence
```

### Execution sequence




For the execution sequence of for loops, note that the different parts of
the heading are used at different times:

- When starting the statement, the initialization is done, and then
  the test of condition (boolean expression).
- After finishing the body and returning to the heading, the iteration operations
  are done, followed by the test.

```{index} statement; break and continue
```

(break-continue)=

```{index} break and continue Statements; string indexing; string length
```



```{index} break and continue Statements
```

## `break` and `continue` Statements




`break` exits the nearest enclosing loop. Execution resumes after that loop. `continue` skips the remaining body and proceeds to the next update/condition check. Decisions inside loops can select when either action occurs. Method returns are taught in Chapter 5 and are not needed here.

Before searching text, introduce its two access operations: `text.Length` counts UTF-16 code units, and `text[i]` reads one `char` at zero-based index `i`. Index zero is first; the last valid index is `text.Length - 1`. An empty string has length zero and no valid index. Use ordinary English letters/digits in these examples; some Unicode characters occupy multiple `char` values.

The next examples search a string directly, without requiring arrays or the later Strings and Their Methods lesson.


string text = "INV-204";
char target = '-';
bool found = false;
int foundIndex = -1;

for (int i = 0; i < text.Length; i++)   // loop for text.Length times
{
   if (text[i] == target)               // if one character == target
   {
      found = true;                    // set found to true
      foundIndex = i;
      break;                           // break out of the enclosing loop
   }
}

if (found)                             // if found == true (from the previous block)
{
   Console.WriteLine("Target found at index " + foundIndex);
}
else
{
   Console.WriteLine("Target not found");
}


When `text[i]` matches `target`, `break` stops the loop and the program reports the found index. Change the text to `INV204` or an empty string to check unsuccessful search. The alternate implementation below includes `!found` in the loop condition instead of using `break`.


string text = "INV-204";
char target = '-';
bool found = false;
int foundIndex = -1;

for (int i = 0; i < text.Length && !found; i++) {
   if (text[i] == target) {
      found = true;
      foundIndex = i;
   }
}

if (found) {
   Console.WriteLine("Target found at index " + foundIndex);
} else {
   Console.WriteLine("Target not found");
}


As you can see, the code exit because the condition section of the if statement header
has an expression `!found` ({ref}`logical-operators`), meaning found is not true.
The shows that since `break` statements rely on the logic of the conditional statement,
if the condition can be embedded in the header of the loop, you don't have to use break.
However, if you are designing a loop that has multiple exit criteria, using break statements
can make the code much less verbose in the header's condition section, and hence easier to
follow because the if statement conditions and the immediate break action may be clearly
presented.

## Nested `for` Loop




There will be times when **nested** loops are are required for the problem scenario.
A nested loop can look like this:



```text
outer-Loop
{
   // body of outer-loop
   inner-Loop
   {
      // body of inner-loop
   }
... ... ...
}
```


Continuing with our discussion on `break`, let's say we are in a situation like the following:



```text
for (....) {

   // some statements of outer for loop

   for (....) {
      ...
      if (...) {
      ...
      break;
      }
      ...
   }

   // some statements of outer for look
}
```


The break statement is in the inner loop. If it is reached, the inner loop ends,
but the **inner loop** is just a **single statement** inside the outer loop,
and **the outer loop continues**.
If the outer loop continuation condition remains true,
the inner loop will be executed again. As an example:



for (int i = 0; i <= 3; i++)
{
   for (int j = 0; j <= 3; j++)
   {

      if (i == 2)
      {
         break;
      }

      Console.WriteLine("{0} -- {1}", i, j);
   }
}



Can you determine the output of the preceding code? Try it with `csharprepl`, `Run C#`, or a test project
in your tests folder.

`continue` Statement

For completeness we mention the much less used `continue` statement:

> `continue;`

A `continue` statement:
\- does not break out of the whole loop statement.
\- break/skips the execution of the rest of the *body* in the current enclosing loop iteration.
\- starts the next enclosing loop iteration.

In the simplest situations, a `continue` statement just avoids an extra `else` clause.
It can considerably shorten code if the test is inside of complicated, deeply nested
`if` statements. As an example:



for (int i = 0; i <= 3; i++)
{
   for (int j = 0; j <= 3; j++)
   {
      if (i == 2)
      {
           continue;
      }

      Console.WriteLine("{0} -- {1}", i, j);
   }
}

in your tests folder.

## `foreach` Statement




A string can supply characters to a loop. For these introductory examples, use ordinary English letters, digits, and punctuation. `text.Length` is the number of UTF-16 code units, and `text[i]` reads one `char` at zero-based index `i`. The valid indexes run from zero through `text.Length - 1`; an empty string has length zero and no valid index. Some Unicode characters require more than one `char`.

A counted loop visits the positions:

```csharp
string text = "ABC";
for (int i = 0; i < text.Length; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine(text[i]);
}
```

A `foreach` visits the values without managing an index:

```csharp
string text = "ABC";
foreach (char letter in text)
{
    Console.WriteLine(letter);
}
```

Both print A, B, and C on separate lines. `foreach` is useful when each value receives the same treatment; an indexed loop is useful when positions or reverse order matter. Strings are immutable sequences, not arrays. Arrays and other collections follow in Chapters 7-8. Cleaning, searching, and extracting text are developed in Chapter 5; none is required here.

## Formatting Tables




Reports commonly include tables, often with successive lines generated by
a consistent formula and therefore a good example for coding. As a simple first table, we can show the square,
cube, and square root of numbers 1 through 10.
The Math class has a method `Sqrt`, so we take the square root with the `Math.Sqrt`
method. The pattern is consistent, so we can loop easily:



for ( int n = 1; n <= 10; n++)
{
    Console.WriteLine("{0} {1} {2} {3}", n, n*n, n*n*n, Math.Sqrt(n));
}



The numbers will be there, but the output is not pretty:

```none
1 1 1 1
2 4 8 1.4142135623731
3 9 27 1.73205080756888
4 16 64 2
5 25 125 2.23606797749979
6 36 216 2.44948974278318
7 49 343 2.64575131106459
8 64 512 2.82842712474619
9 81 729 3
10 100 1000 3.16227766016838
```

First we might not need all those digits in the square root approximations.
We can replace `{3}` by `{3:F4}` to just show 4 decimal places.

We can adjust the spacing to make nice
columns by using a further formatting option. The longest entries are all
in the last row, where they take up, 2, 3, 4, and 6 columns (for 3.1623).
Change the format string:



for ( int n = 1; n <= 10; n++) {
    Console.WriteLine("{0,2} {1,3} {2,4} {3,6:F4}",
                       n, n*n, n*n*n, Math.Sqrt(n));
}



and we generate the neater output:

```none
 1   1    1 1.0000
 2   4    8 1.4142
 3   9   27 1.7321
 4  16   64 2.0000
 5  25  125 2.2361
 6  36  216 2.4495
 7  49  343 2.6458
 8  64  512 2.8284
 9  81  729 3.0000
10 100 1000 3.1623
```

We are using two new formatting forms:

> `{`
>
> index
>
> `,`
>
> fieldWidth
>
> `}`
>
>  and
>
> `{`
>
> index
>
> `,`
>
> fieldWidth
>
> `:F`
>
> #
>
> `}`

where index, fieldWidth, and # are replaces by specific literal integers.
The new part with the comma (not colon) and fieldWidth, sets the *minimum*
number of columns used for the substituted string, padding with blanks as needed.

*If the string to be inserted is wider than the fieldWidth,*
then the *whole* string is inserted, *ignoring* the fieldWidth. For example:



string s = "stuff";
Console.WriteLine("123456789");
Console.WriteLine("{0,9}\n{0,7}\n{0,5}\n{0,3}", s);



generates:

```none
123456789
    stuff
  stuff
stuff
stuff
```

filling 9, 7, and then 5 columns, by padding with 4, 2, and 0 blanks.
*The last line sticks out past the proposed 3-column fieldWidth.*

One more thing to add to our power table is a heading. We might want:

```none
n   square    cube    root
```

To make the data line up with the heading titles,
we can expand the columns, with code in example:



Console.WriteLine("{0,2}{1,7}{2,5}{3,7}",
              "n", "square", "cube", "root");
for ( int n = 1; n <= 10; n++) {
Console.WriteLine("{0,2}{1,7}{2,5}{3,7:F4}",
                    n, n*n, n*n*n, Math.Sqrt(n));
}



generating the output:

```none

 1       1       1  1.0000
 2       4       8  1.4142
 3       9      27  1.7321
 4      16      64  2.0000
 5      25     125  2.2361
 6      36     216  2.4495
 7      49     343  2.6458
 8      64     512  2.8284
 9      81     729  3.0000
10     100    1000  3.1623
```

Note how we make sure the columns are consistent in the heading and further rows:
We used a format string for the headings with the same field widths as
in the body of the table. A separate variation: We also reduced the length
of the format string by putting all the substitution expressions in braces
right beside each other, and generate the space between columns with a
larger field width.

```

# Greatest Common Divisor

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```


This supporting lesson preserves the full 2025 mathematical development and comparison of brute-force, subtraction, remainder, and recursive approaches. The loop algorithms accept positive integers; the remainder and recursive variants also accept a single zero. The method listings are for revisiting after Chapter 5; recursion is a preview to revisit in Chapters 17 and 22.

These explanations and tasks retain the earlier CS1 teaching material.[^0404_gcd-restored]


- This section is kept here for your reference to looping in the future.

```{index} Euclid's Algorithm
```

## Euclid's Algorithm




```{index} Euclid's Algorithm
```

The greatest common divisor of two non-zero integers is a great example
to illustrate the power of loops. Everyone learns about the *concept* of
a greatest common divisor when faced with a fraction that is not in
*reduced* form.

Consider the fraction {math}`\frac{2}{4}`, which is the same as {math}`\frac{1}{2}`.
The fraction {math}`\frac{2}{4}` can be reduced, because the numerator and
denominator both have greatest common factor of 2. That is,
{math}`\frac{2}{4} = \frac{1 \cdot 2}{2 \cdot 2}`. So the factor of 2 can be
canceled from both the numerator and the denominator.

Euclid (the mathematician from classic times and author of *Elements*)
is credited with having come up with a clever algorithm for how to
compute the greatest common divisor efficiently. It is written as
follows, where {math}`a \bmod b` means `a % b` in C#.


```{math}
gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a \bmod b)
```



```{math}
gcd(a, 0) = a
```


It is common in mathematics to list functions as one or more *cases*.
The way you read this is as follows:

- In general, the greatest common divisor of `a` and `b` is the same as
  computing the greatest common divisor of `b` and the remainder of `a`
  divided by `b`.
- In the case where `b` is zero, the result is `a`. This makes sense
  because `a` divides itself and 0.

To gain some appreciation of how the definition *always* allows you to
compute the greatest common divisor, it is worthwhile to try it out for
a couple of numbers where you *know* the greatest common divisor. For
example, we already know that the greatest common divisor of 10 and 15
is 5. Let's use Euclid's method to verify this:

- {math}`gcd(10, 15) = gcd(15, 10 \bmod 15) = gcd(15, 10)`
- {math}`gcd(15, 10) = gcd(10, 15 \bmod 10) = gcd(10, 5)`
- {math}`gcd(10, 5) = gcd(5, 10 \bmod 5) = gcd(5, 0)`
- {math}`gcd(5, 0) = 5`

Notice that in the example above, the first number (10) was smaller than
the second (15), and the first transformation just swapped the numbers,
so the larger number was first. Thereafter the first number is always
larger.

```{index} GCD "Brute Force" Method
```

## GCD "Brute Force" Method




```{index} GCD "Brute Force" Method
```

Now that we've gotten the preliminaries out of the way and have a basic
mathematical explanation for how to calculate the greatest common
divisor, we'll take a look at how to translate this into code using the
machinery of while loops that you've recently learned.

The way GCD is formulated above is, indeed, the most clever way to
calculate the greatest common divisor. Yet the way we learn about the
greatest common divisor in elementary school (at least at first) is to
learn how to factor the numbers a and b, often in a brute force way. So
for example, when calculating the greatest common divisor of 10 and 15,
we can immediately see it, because we know that both of these numbers
are divisible by 5 (e.g. 5 \* 2 = 10 and 5 \* 3 = 15). So the greatest
common divisor is 5.

But if we had something more tricky to do like 810 and 729, we might
have to think a bit more.

Before we learn to find the factors of numbers, we will often just
"try" numbers until we get the greatest common divisor. This sort of
trial process can take place in a loop, where we start at 1 and end at
min(a, b). Why the minimum? We know that none of the values after the
minimum can divide both a and b (in integer division), because no larger
number can divide a smaller positive number. The smaller number would be
the (non-zero) remainder.

Now take a look at a basic version of GCD:

``` csharp
/// Return the greatest common divisor of positive numbers.
public static int GreatestCommonDivisor (int a, int b)
{
   int n = Math.Min (a, b);
   int gcd = 1, i = 1;

   while (i <= n) {
      if (a % i == 0 && b % i == 0) {
         gcd = i;
      }
      i++;
   }
   return gcd;
}
//
```

This code works as follows:

- We begin by finding `Math.Min(a, b)`. This is how to compute the
  minimum of any two values in C#. Technically, we don't need to use
  the minimum of a and b, but there is no point in doing any more work
  than necessary.
- We'll use the variable `i` as the loop index, starting at 1.
- The variable `gcd` will hold the largest currently known common
  divisor. We start with 1, which divides any integer, and we will look
  for a higher value that also divides a and b.
- The line `while (i <= n)` is used to indicate that we are iterating
  the values of `i` until the minimum of `a` and `b` (computed earlier)
  is reached.
- The line `if (a % i == 0 && b % i == 0)` is used to check whether we
  have found a new value that replaces our previous *candidate* for the
  GCD. A value can only be a candidate for the GCD if it divides a and b
  without a remainder. The modulus operator `%` is our way of
  determining whether there is a remainder from the division operation
  `a / i` or `b / i`.
- The line `i++` is our way of going to the next value of `i` to be
  tested as the new GCD.
- When this loop terminates, the greatest common divisor has been found.

So this gives you a relatively straightforward way of calculating the
greatest common divisor. While simple, it is not necessarily the most
efficient way of determining the GCD. If you think about what is going
on, this loop could run a significant number of times. For example, if
you were calculating the GCD two very large numbers, say, one billion
(1,000,000,000) and two billion (2,000,000,000) it is painfully evident
that you would consider a large number of values (a billion, in fact)
before obtaining the candidate GCD, which we know is 1,000,000,000.

```{index} Brute-Force GCD Exercise
```

### Brute-Force GCD Exercise




```{index} Brute-Force GCD Exercise
```

The code above goes through all integers 1 through `min(a, b)`. That is
not generally necessary when the GCD is greater than 1, even with a
brute-force mindset. Write a `g_c_d_basic_faster.cs` to do this with a
slightly different `GreatestCommonDivisor` function.[^0404_gcd-1]

```{index} GCD Subtraction Method
```

## GCD Subtraction Method




```{index} GCD Subtraction Method
```

The subtraction method (also attributable to Euclid) to compute the
Greatest Common Divisor works as follows:

- Based on the *mathematical* definition in the previous section, the
  greatest common divisor algorithm saves a step when we already have
  `a` and `b` in the *right order*.
- The *right order* means that {math}`a > b`. As we noted earlier, the
  cleverness of the *mathematical* definition is that `a` and `b` are
  swapped as the first step to ensure that {math}`a > b`, after which we can
  repeatedly divide to get the GCD.
- Division, of course, is a form of repetitive subtraction, so the way
  to divide by `b` is to repeatedly subtract it (from a) until `a` is no
  longer greater than `b`.
- The subtraction method basically makes no attempt to put `a` and `b`
  in the right order. Instead, we just write similar loops to allow for
  the possibility of either order.
- A simple check must be performed to ensure that the approach of
  repeated subtraction actually resulted in the GCD. This will happen if
  `a` and `b` bump into one another, thereby meaning that we have
  computed the GCD.

``` csharp
public static int GreatestCommonDivisor (int a, int b)
{
   int c;
   while (a != b) {
      while (a > b) {
         c = a - b;
         a = c;
      }
      while (b > a) {
         c = b - a;
         b = c;
      }
   }
   return a;
}
//
```

A look at the source code more or less follows the above explanation.

Let's start by looking at the inner loop at line 5, `while (a > b)`. In
this loop, we are repeatedly subtracting `b` from `a`, which we know we
can do, because `a` started out as being larger than `b`. At the end of
loop `a` is reduced to either

1.  `b`, in which case `b` exactly divided the earlier `a`, and `b` is
    the GCD, or
2.  a number less than `b`, namely {math}`a \bmod b` (or in C# terms `a % b`),
    and the process continues\....

The loop on line 9 is similar to the loop in line 5. For the same
reasons as we already explained, `b` ends up equal to `a`, which is the
GCD, or `b` ends up as {math}`b \bmod a`.

As discussed above, if `a` and `b` end up as the same number, that is
the GCD. On the other hand, the first GCD algorithm example showed how
remainders may need to be to be calculated over and over. The outer loop
in this version keeps this up until `a` and `b` are reduced to equal
values. At this point the inner loops would make no further changes, and
the common value is the GCD.

As an exercise to the reader, you may want to consider adding some
`Console.WriteLine()` statements to print the values of `a` and `b`
within each loop, and after both loops have executed. It will allow you
to see in visual terms how this method does its work.

```{index} GCD Remainder Loop
```

## GCD Remainder Loop




```{index} GCD Remainder Loop
```

There are several ways to code the shorter Euclidean algorithm at the
beginning of this GCD section. It is a repetitive pattern, and a loop
can be used. There are two parameters, `a` and `b`, to the gcd, and they
can be successively changed, suggesting a loop. What is the continuation
condition? You stop when `b` is 0, so you continue while `b != 0`. The
parameters `a` and `b` need to be replaced by `b` and `a % b`. One extra
variable needs to be introduced to make this double change work. The
simplest is to introduce a variable `r` for the remainder. Check and see
for yourself that you need an extra variable like `r`:

    /// Return the greatest common divisor of nonnegative numbers,
    /// not both 0.
    public static int GreatestCommonDivisor (int a, int b)
    {
       while (b != 0) {
          int r = a % b;
          a = b;
          b = r;
       }
       return a;
    } 

More verbose demonstration code, that prints the progress each time
through loop is in `g_c_d_remainder_loop/g_c_d_remainder_loop.cs`.

```{index} Preview: Recursive GCD
```

## Preview: Recursive GCD




```{index} Preview: Recursive GCD
```

The first statement of Euclid's algorithm said (in C#) when :

    gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)

It is saying the result of the function with one set of parameters is
equal to calling the function with another set of parameters. If we put
this into a C# function definition, it would mean the instructions for
the function say to *call itself*. This is a broadly useful technique
called *recursion*, where a function calls *itself* inside its
definition. We don't expect you to master this technique immediately
but do feel that it is important you at least *hear* about it and see
its tremendous power:

    /// Return the greatest common divisor of nonnegative numbers,
    /// not both 0.
    public static int GreatestCommonDivisor (int a, int b)
    {
       if (b == 0) {                               // base
          return a;                                //   case
       } else {
          return GreatestCommonDivisor (b, a % b); // recursion
       }
    }

- Recalling our earlier definition, the case {math}`gcd(a, 0) = a` is handled
  directly by lines commented as "base case".
- And the case {math}`gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a \bmod b)` is handled by line with
  comment "recursion", with the function calling itself.

In `g_c_d_euclid_recursive/g_c_d_euclid_recursive.cs` is a wordier
demonstration version that prints to the screen the progress at each
recursive call.

The recursive version of the `gcd` function *refers to itself* by
*calling* itself. Though this seems circular, you can see from the
examples that it works very well. The important point is that the calls
to the same function are not completely the same: *Successive* calls
have *smaller* second numbers, and the second number eventually reaches
0, and in that case there is a direct final answer. Hence the function
is not really circular.

This recursive version is a much more direct translation of the original
mathematical algorithm than the looping version!

The general idea of recursion is for a function to call itself with
*simpler* parameters, until a simple enough place is reached, where the
answer can be directly calculated.

```{index} Run the Loop Now
```

## Run the Loop Now




```{index} Run the Loop Now
```

For the current chapter, the same remainder updates can be written as top-level statements. Save the remainder before changing `a`; otherwise `a % b` would use the changed value. Trace `(810, 729)`, `(10, 15)`, and `(15, 10)`. Compare the number of iterations with trial division and subtraction. The common divisor is unchanged by each remainder step; the second value strictly decreases after the initial swap until it becomes zero.

using System;
int a = 810, b = 729;
while (b != 0) {
    Console.WriteLine($"a={a}, b={b}");
    int remainder = a % b;
    a = b;
    b = remainder;
}
Console.WriteLine($"GCD = {a}");

(defining-own-functions)= # Methods You already call built-in methods, make decisions, and repeat work with loops. Now you will define your own methods to name and reuse those familiar operations. Long programs become unmanageable when all code lives in one place. Methods let you name a block of code, give it inputs, return a result, and reuse the same logic from multiple places. - **Method definition**: A method packages a named task so the program can call it when needed. - **Method header and contract**: The full declaration communicates call syntax; the contract states the required behavior. The C# signature is the narrower method identity used for overloading. - **Parameters**: Parameters let one method work with different input values. - **Return values**: A value-returning method computes a result that other code can store or combine. Methods are the first major step from writing a script toward designing a program. They make code easier to read, test, debug, and extend.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: IPpEefuFiVM :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[C# methods 📞](https://youtube.com/watch?v=IPpEefuFiVM)* by Bro Code. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Define methods with clear names, parameters, and return types 2. Call methods and use their return values in larger expressions 3. Design method signatures that communicate intent clearly 4. Distinguish between `void` methods and value-returning methods 5. Use methods to remove repetition and organize program logic 6. Call string methods to clean, search, and extract parts of text

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`5.1. Designing and Calling Methods <0501_intro_methods>` - {doc}`5.2. Method Parameters <0503_parameter>` - {doc}`5.3. Returned Results and Method Contracts <0502_signature_call>` - {doc}`5.4. Strings and Their Methods <0504_strings>` - {doc}`5.5. Composition, Refactoring, and Method Checks <0505_summary>`

Glossary

| # | Term | Explanation | |---:|---|---| | 1 | Method | A named block of code that performs a task and can be called from elsewhere. | | 2 | Method call | An instruction that runs a method. | | 3 | Parameter | A named input listed in a method definition. | | 4 | Argument | A value supplied to a parameter during a method call. | | 5 | Return type | The type of value a method sends back to its caller. | | 6 | Return value | The actual value produced by a value-returning method. | | 7 | Void method | A method that performs an action but does not return a value. | | 8 | Signature | The method name together with its parameter list. | | 9 | Scope | The region of code where a name can be used. | | 10 | Local variable | A variable declared inside a method or block. | | 11 | Helper method | A smaller method used to organize part of a larger task. | | 12 | Refactoring | Changing code structure without changing its intended behavior. |

content.chapters/05_methods/0501_intro_methods: (a-first-function)= # Designing and Calling Methods ```{contents} :local: :depth: 2 ``` ```{index} Discover a Task Before Naming a Method ``` ```{index} Discover a Task Before Naming a Method ``` ## Discover a Task Before Naming a Method A method boundary should express a responsibility that a caller can understand. Imagine an invoice program that reads a quantity, computes a line amount, adds a packing fee, and prints a report. These actions are related, but they do not all need the same information or have the same effects. Separating them lets a calculation be checked without simulating keyboard input or capturing console output. Write a short sentence for each proposed task. Then identify the information that varies, what the caller needs back, and which effects are intentional. A method named Process does not tell a reader whether it calculates, prints, changes stock, or does all three. A name such as LineTotal makes a more specific promise when accompanied by its price/quantity contract. | Proposed task | Inputs | Useful result | Intentional external effect | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Calculate line total | Unit price and quantity | Decimal amount | None | | Format receipt line | Description and amount | String | None | | Display receipt | Formatted text | No returned value | Console output | The table is a design tool, not a rule that every program must contain precisely these three methods. A very small program may keep printing in the caller. A reusable formatting policy may deserve a method even when it is initially called once. Repetition is one reason for extraction; giving a complicated idea a clear name is another. A common mistake is to extract a group of adjacent lines simply because they are adjacent. Instead ask whether they share one coherent purpose and whether the proposed interface hides irrelevant details. If callers need to know every internal step, the boundary may not be helping them. Guided decision: should CalculateDiscount read a customer name from the keyboard? Under a calculation-only contract, no. The caller obtains input and passes the values required by the rule. This makes the same calculation usable from a console program, a test, or a future interface without rewriting its arithmetic. For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading] ```{index} function; definition ``` ```{index} Introduction ``` ```{index} A Repeated Task Needs a Name ``` ```{index} A Repeated Task Needs a Name ``` (methods-reuse)= ## A Repeated Task Needs a Name ```{index} A Repeated Task Needs a Name ``` A shop prints a store name and separator on every receipt. Copying those two statements for every receipt works at first, but a store-name change must then be made in several places. A method names the task once so callers can reuse it. This is **decomposition**: divide a larger program into understandable responsibilities. Before refactoring, the statements appear twice: ```text print store name print separator print store name print separator ``` After refactoring, two calls use one definition. Predict the output: defining the helper does not print anything by itself. using System; PrintHeader(); PrintHeader(); static void PrintHeader() { Console.WriteLine("Campus Books"); Console.WriteLine("------------"); } The two-line header appears twice, in call order. Change the store name in the definition and run again: both calls use that change. Add a third call without copying the body. This demonstrates reuse rather than merely asserting that reuse is useful. ```{figure} ../../figures/method_decomposition.svg :alt: Two repeated sets of receipt-header statements become two calls to one PrintHeader definition. A task name connects each caller to one definition. ``` Read the left column as duplicated instructions and the right as named calls. A method does not automatically make a program better; it should express a coherent responsibility. Separate calculation, input, and presentation when those have different jobs. ```{index} Connect Calls, Definitions, and Program Forms ``` ```{index} Connect Calls, Definitions, and Program Forms ``` (method-program-forms)= ## Connect Calls, Definitions, and Program Forms ```{index} Connect Calls, Definitions, and Program Forms ``` You already consume methods such as `Math.Round` and `Console.WriteLine`. Now you supply a definition so a caller can ask your code to do work. The caller needs a contract: what arguments are required, what result is returned, and what effects occur. This chapter uses top-level statements with explicitly `static` local helper functions for most runnable examples. A **local function** is a named function inside the compiler-generated entry method in this program form. It has no `public` modifier. An explicit static class-member method instead lives inside a class and may use an access modifier. Both forms can demonstrate input, return, and execution flow, but they are not interchangeable declarations. | Task | Top-level teaching form | Explicit class-based project form | | --- | --- | --- | | Begin the program | First top-level statement | First statement in the selected Main | | Define a helper | `static void PrintHeader() { ... }` beside top-level statements | Same helper inside Program | | Call it | `PrintHeader();` | Call from Main or another permitted method | | Explain the wrapper | The compiler supplies the entry method | The source shows Main and Program | Use one program form at a time in a file. The original class-based examples are retained as console-project reference versions; do not paste them after a complete top-level program. This distinction explains the layout sketch and static/instance terminology that follow. It is not yet a lesson in designing objects. Methods/functions are reusable, callable, and customizable pieces of code in a computer program. When a function is a part of a class, it is called a method. Class-member functions are called methods. C# also supports local functions, including helpers declared alongside top-level statements, so the program form matters. It is, therefore, by definition, more accurate to call these subroutines methods rather than functions in C# since C# is an OOP language. However, when discussing the construct of subroutine in general, the general term **function** seems appropriate and you will see people use the terms interchangeably from time to time. In C# or other object oriented programming (OOP) languages, methods are usually associated with a class. In other languages, you may hear the term function. A function is similar to a method, but it is not tied to a class. Due to the similarity in overall usage, it is common to use the terms methods and functions as synonyms. ```text Method (class member) Local function Standalone function (inside method) (other languages) +-----------------------+ +--------------------------+ +-----------------------+ | class Program | | class Program | | [code...] | | { | | { | | int add(int a, int b) | | static int Add(...) | | static void Main() | | { | | { return a + b; } | | { | | return a + b; | | } | | int Add(...) { ... } | | } | +-----------------------+ | } | | [code...] | | } | +-----------------------+ +--------------------------+ ``` You have seen the **Main()** method in C# console app programs generated using the .NET template with `--use-program-main`. In the traditional class-based style, the Main() method is the application’s entry point. When the application is run, execution begins at the start of the Main() method. In modern C#, programs may also use top-level statements without an explicit Main() method. Up until this unit, you wrote the program steps in top-level statements or an explicit Main method, but now you will be creating new methods that can be called by the main method. Methods are **named** code blocks that can be reused (called) whenever we needed. Methods are an **abstraction** of your code because methods abstract away details (you use the methods by their names only) and that serves to organize your code by function and reduce the repetition of code. In addition, it helps with debugging and maintenance since changes to that block of code only need to happen in one place. Here are some of the main reasons to use multiple methods in your programs: - Reusing Code: Avoid repetition of code. - Reducing Complexity: Divide a problem into sub-problems to solve it a piece at a time. - Maintainability and Debugging: Smaller and specific code blocks are easier to trace and debug. Also, you only need to maintain one piece of code even if it's used all over the place. When you see duplicate lines of code, that is a signal for you to make a new method. A method is a named set of statements. When we want to execute the statements, we **call** the method using its name. Methods are called in two different ways: - **Instance methods**: methods that are called using an object, referred to as instance methods or object methods. - **static methods**: the methods in this unit are called without an object, so they are static methods. Static methods are also referred to as **class methods**. Some important characteristics of methods/functions are: - **SRP**: In general, a method should do a single thing, which we call single responsibility principle (SRP). - **Method composition**: You combine a sequence of simple methods to build more complex desired behavior. - **Method call**: A method body runs when it is **called**. We say we are making a “**function call**” or “method call” when we invoke/use the subroutine. - **Arguments**: When calling a method, we often pass data into the method. The data passed to the method are called arguments. - **Parameters**: The variables in the method heading defined to receive those arguments are called parameters. - **Return**: We usually design the method to return values when called. The short cell below runs as top-level statements. The following project version shows the same work in an explicit Main method; it is included so you can connect this chapter to earlier console-project examples. using System; Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!"); ::::{dropdown} Class-based console-project version The top-level example above is the version to run as a standalone notebook cell. This complete project version retains the explicit `Main` structure. Save it as the only program in a separate console project; do not paste it after top-level statements in the same file. ```csharp namespace MethodDemo; class Program { static void Main(string[] args) { Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!"); } } ``` :::: From the `MethodDemo` project folder, run `dotnet run`. The .NET runtime starts `Main` automatically; you do not add a separate call to `Program.Main`. The program prints: ```text Hello, World! ``` The Main method, however, is unique by design because it is designated to be the entry point of an application. Although you can write code in the Main method, you will learn how to write methods in addition to, and outside of, the Main method to extend the functionality of your code. ```{important} **One entry point (the `Main()` method) per project, but a project can have many `.cs` files.** Each executable project selects one entry point. Only one file may contain top-level statements; an explicit Main can instead be selected when no top-level statements are present. However, a project can include as many additional `.cs` files as needed; those files simply define extra classes and methods that `Main()` calls. For these exercises, put independently runnable programs in separate projects. A project can technically contain multiple candidate Main methods when its startup object is explicitly configured, but that is not needed here. ``` ```{index} Guided Practice: Reuse a Notice ``` ```{index} Guided Practice: Reuse a Notice ``` ## Guided Practice: Reuse a Notice ```{index} Guided Practice: Reuse a Notice ``` Define a no-argument helper that prints `Returns accepted within 30 days.` Call it twice. Then change the message once and confirm both calls change. Keep this printing method void. // Exercise: Guided Practice: Reuse a Notice // exercise-id: cscs-methods-guided-m5-a68bc782 using System; PrintNotice(); PrintNotice(); static void PrintNotice() { // Your code starts here. // Your code ends here. } // Solution: Guided Practice: Reuse a Notice using System; PrintNotice(); PrintNotice(); static void PrintNotice() { Console.WriteLine("Returns accepted within 30 days."); } ```{index} Designing Methods ``` ## Designing Methods A caller needs a result without repeating the calculation. Start by stating the method's job, input types, result type, and assumptions. Then write a definition and calls that check that contract. In this section, keep the question “what does the caller receive?” separate from “what appears on the screen?” For a simple integer square, the contract is: accept an integer in a range whose square fits in int, return its square, and print nothing inside the calculation. We use small inputs here; arbitrary large integers need a stated overflow policy. ```{index} Method Signature ``` ```{index} Method Signature ``` ## Method Signature One method you encountered in the explicit class-based C# program form is Main, in which *Main* is the name that you can refer to this set of statements. A Main method is special because it is designated as the only entry point of a C# application and its selected entry point begins the console program [^0502_signature_call-1]. Note that the **Main method** is contained in a **class** (Program), which is a standard arrangement for OOP languages. You define a method by writing the method’s **header** and **body**. The **header** is the complete declaration line. For C# overload identity, the **signature** identifies the name, generic arity when present, and parameter types/passing modes; it does not include the return type or parameter names. [^0502_signature_call-2] When defining methods, you follow a recipe (standard syntax) for the **method definition**. The class-member definition pattern is as follows: [^0502_signature_call-3] ``` none [AccessModifier] static ReturnTypeOrVoid MethodName(ParameterList) { // Method Body: a set of statements enclosed in curly braces { } } ``` The complete header and body have the following parts: | Header component | Description | | --- | --- | | Access Level | Optional. This determines visibility of methods between classes, It does not determine whether code can instantiate objects. For a local helper, omit access modifiers. For a class-member helper, choose visibility appropriate to its callers. | | Static modifier | In the form taught here, define the method as a static member method of the class. When not defined as static, it is an instance member. | | Return Type | If the method is returning a value, this indicates what data type it will be. Not all methods return values. Methods that do not return a value have a return type of `void`. | | Method Name | The method’s `identifier`; class-member overloads may share a name with different signatures. This is what you use to call your method. | | Parameter List | A parameter is a placeholder for specific data that the method will act upon. Parameters are optional. In these cases, the `()` are still part of the method call, but remain empty. | | Method Body | This is where you code your method. Note it is contained between `{}`. | With method signatures, you can design methods specifically to your needs. But for now, let us analyze the two methods in class TryMethods below to apply our understanding of headers and calls: using System; MyMethod(); static void MyMethod() { Console.WriteLine("IST 1551"); Console.WriteLine("T.Y. Chen"); } ::::{dropdown} Class-based console-project version The top-level example above is the version to run as a standalone notebook cell. This complete project version retains the explicit `Main` structure. Save it as the only program in a separate console project; do not paste it after top-level statements in the same file. ```csharp using System; // the using statement #pragma warning disable CS7022 class TryMethods // class declaration { public static void Main(){ MyMethod(); // invoking MyMethod from Main } // public static void Main(string[] args) // static modifier, return modifier, and method name // { // static: can be invoked directly; void, no return to caller // MyMethod(); // method MyMethod (line# 9) is called // } public static void MyMethod() // static modifier, return modifier, and method name { // static: can be invoked directly; void, no return to caller Console.WriteLine("IST 1551"); // Method body Console.WriteLine("T.Y. Chen"); // Method body } } #pragma warning restore CS7022 ``` :::: You have probably noticed that you can prepare this code by making the **MyMethod** project folder (`mkdir MyMethod`), then creating the project by running `dotnet new console --use-program-main` (or just do `dotnet new console` then change the code to include the `Main method`). After that, you run `code .` from the terminal to open the project in VS Code and click on Program.cs to edit the source code. ```{index} Method Calls & Returns ``` ```{index} Method Calls & Returns ``` ## Method Calls & Returns The runnable cell calls MyMethod from top-level statements. The retained class-based version makes the same call inside Main. The call is MyMethod(), not a call to Main. When making a method call, you use the method **name** followed by **parentheses**. The method header `static void MyMethod()` indicates the return type is `void` and there are no formal parameters, which means you can call it simply by writing `MyMethod();`. An important feature of functions/methods is that they can **return** values to their **callers**. In the example below, `SquareTheNumber(int num)` is defined with a return type of `int` and is called directly from the top-level code, passing a parameter. using System; int digit = 4; int squaredNum = SquareTheNumber(digit); int squaredAndSummed = squaredNum + SquareTheNumber(digit); Console.WriteLine(squaredNum); Console.WriteLine(squaredAndSummed); Console.WriteLine(SquareTheNumber(5)); static int SquareTheNumber(int num) { return num * num; } ::::{dropdown} Class-based console-project version The top-level example above is the version to run as a standalone notebook cell. This complete project version retains the explicit `Main` structure. Save it as the only program in a separate console project; do not paste it after top-level statements in the same file. ```csharp using System; class Program { static int SquareTheNumber(int num) { return num * num; // the value to be returned is given by the expression in the return statement. } static void Main(){ int digit = 4; int squaredNum = SquareTheNumber(digit); int squaredAndSummed = squaredNum + SquareTheNumber(digit); Console.WriteLine(squaredNum); Console.WriteLine(squaredAndSummed); Console.WriteLine(SquareTheNumber(5)); } } ``` :::: In this example: - `return num * num;` computes the value that replaces this call in the caller. - `digit` starts at 4. Passing it binds the value 4 to `num`. - `squaredNum` is a variable, not a method; it stores the returned 16. - The addition uses `squaredNum` plus a second call with digit still equal to 4: 16 + 16 = 32. - The final call uses 5 and returns 25. The three printed values are 16, 32, and 25. The return type must agree with the returned expression through an allowed conversion. `void` means no returned value; it does not mean the method cannot print or have another effect. ```{index} Flow of execution ``` ```{index} Flow of execution ``` ## Flow of execution In terms of the construct of **sequential processing**, functions/methods alter code execution order in several ways: by statements not being executed as the definition is first read, and then when the method is called during execution, jumping to the method code, and back at the end of the method execution. [^0502_signature_call-5] A class can contain multiple methods. It can be tempting to think the methods are executed in the order they appear in the class, but this is not the case. In an explicit class-based console program, ordinary execution begins in the selected Main method; a top-level program begins with its first statement. Each statement in the main is executed sequentially, one at a time, until you reach a method call. A method call causes the program execution to jump to the first line of the called method. Each statement in the called method is then executed in order. When the called method finishes, execution returns to the point in its caller that was waiting for the result. The caller may itself be another helper. [^0502_signature_call-6] In other words, the order in which the method definition code blocks does not matter to C#. It is a human choice. One good practice is to show `Main` first. This means a human reading in order gets an overview of what is happening by looking at Main, but does not know the details until reading the definitions of other methods. ```{index} method; summary of syntax ``` ```{index} Static Methods ``` (static-method-summary)= ## Static Methods The reference rules below summarize the chapter, but designing a method also requires judgment. Start from the job, choose inputs and a returned result, state assumptions, then check the implementation independently. Here we refactor the same checkout calculation twice and verify that naming helpers preserves its behavior. | Design question | Chapter connection | | --- | --- | | What coherent job deserves a name? | 5.1 decomposition and reuse | | What inputs/result/effects form the contract? | 5.2 definitions, calls, returns | | What information must cross the call boundary? | 5.3 parameter binding and scope | | What library operations can do part of the work? | 5.4 strings as reusable methods | | How will we know the result is correct? | Independently derived expected values and boundaries | This chapter has introduced static methods: those used in procedural programming as opposed to {ref}`instance-methods` used to implement object-oriented programming. ```{index} Method definition ``` ```{index} Method definition ``` ## Method definition The general syntax for defining a static method is: ```csharp static returnTypeOrVoid MethodName ( parameter_list ) { // statements in the method body... } ``` Things to know about defining a method in C#: 1. **Parameters**: The *parameter list* can be empty or contain one or more comma separated parameter entries. Each parameter entry has the form > type parameterName 2. **Modifier**: For class-member methods, accessibility determines which callers are permitted. `public static` allows access through the type where that type is accessible; other access levels have other rules. Local helpers beside top-level statements do not take an access modifier. 3. **Return Type**: If **returnTypeOrVoid** in the heading is not `void`, each normally completing path must produce a compatible result; the mere presence of one return statement is insufficient. A return statement has the form > `return` *expression* `;` where the expression should be of the same type as in **returnTypeOrVoid**. Execution of the method terminates immediately when a return statement is reached. 4. In the traditional class-based style, execution starts at a method with a heading including > `static void Main` In modern C#, programs may also use *top-level statements* without an explicit `Main` method. ```{index} Method Calls ``` ```{index} Method Calls ``` ## Method Calls 1. A method call takes the form **MethodName** `(` actual parameter list `)` A method call makes the method definition be *executed*. 2. The actual parameter list is a comma separated list of the *same* length as the parameter list. Each entry is an expression. The entries in an actual parameter list do *not* include type declarations. Effectively, the method execution starts by assigning to each parameter variable the corresponding value from evaluating the actual parameter expression. In particular, that means the actual parameter values must be allowed in an assignment statement for a variable of the parameter's type! 3. If the method has return type `void`, it can only be used syntactically as an entire statement (with a semicolon added). After the method call completes, execution continues with the next statement. 4. If there is a non-void return type, then the method call is syntactically an expression in the statement where it appears. The execution of such a method must reach a return statement. The value of the method-call expression is the value of the expression in this return statement. 5. A method with a return value can also legally be used as a whole statement. In this case the return value is lost. Though legal, this is often an error! ```{rubric} Footnotes ``` [^0502_signature_call-1]: Note that if you have more than one candidate Main method, use the [StartupObject](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/advanced#mainentrypoint-or-startupobject) compiler option to specify which Main method to use as the entry point. [^0502_signature_call-2]: Note that, in OOP, method signature usually refers the method name and the type of its parameters (enclosed in parentheses and separated by commas) while the method header means the whole first line of the method definition. Use header for the complete declaration and signature for the narrower C# identity rule; see [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/basic-concepts). [^0502_signature_call-3]: This template and explanation is adopted from [^0502_signature_call-4]: The compiler can generate an entry method for top-level statements; the source need not explicitly declare Main. ## A Boolean Result Answers a Question



A returned result need not be a number to print. A method can answer a question, and a bool result can become the condition of an if statement. Suppose an order receives free delivery when its subtotal is at least 50. The question is whether an order qualifies, not how much its delivery costs. Keeping those contracts distinct helps explain why two related methods may have different return types.

Trace the boundary: 49.99 does not qualify, 50 qualifies, and 50.01 qualifies. The equality is part of the rule. Writing `>` instead of `>=` would still compile and would pass examples far from the threshold. The boundary cases distinguish the intended rule from that plausible defect.

The general form is `static bool QuestionName(parameterList) { return condition; }`. Here the condition already has type bool. There is no need to convert it into the strings `"true"` and `"false"`; those are text values and cannot serve as an if condition. Printing the answer inside a void method also does not give the caller a Boolean result to use.

Guided variation: qualification additionally requires a nonnegative subtotal. Explain whether that is an input precondition or a condition the method must check. Either design can be explicit, but silently switching between them makes testing and reuse confusing. State the accepted domain before writing your new tests.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


using System;
Console.WriteLine(Qualifies(49.99m));
Console.WriteLine(Qualifies(50m));
Console.WriteLine(Qualifies(50.01m));
static bool Qualifies(decimal subtotal) { return subtotal >= 50m; }

## Returned Values Replace Calls




```{index} Returned Values Replace Calls
```


using System;
Console.WriteLine(F(3));
Console.WriteLine(F(3) + F(4));
static int F(int x) { return x * x; }


You probably have used mathematical functions in algebra class, but
they all had calculated values associated with them. For instance
if you defined

> F(x)=x{sup}`2`

then it follows that F(3) is 3{sup}`2` = 9, and F(3)+F(4) is
3{sup}`2` + 4{sup}`2` = 9 + 16 = 25.

Method calls in expressions get replaced during evaluation by the value of the method.
That's why when we can directly print out (line# 12-13) the result of the method call in the
following code.

The corresponding definition and examples in C# would be the
following:




The C# syntax to notice is the **return statement**, with the word
`return` followed by an expression, value, or variable(s). Methods that return values
can be used in expressions (e.g., line# 13: F(3) + F(4)), just like in math class. When an
expression with a method call is evaluated, the method call is
effectively replaced temporarily by its returned value. Inside the
C# method, the value to be returned is given by the
expression in the `return` statement.

Since the method returns data, and all data in C# is typed,
there must be a type given for the value returned. Note that the
method header does not start with `static void`.
In place of `void` is `int`. The `void` in earlier method header
meant nothing was returned. The `int` here means that a value *is*
returned and its type is `int`.

After the method `F` finishes executing from inside



```csharp
Console.WriteLine(F(3));
```


it is as if the statement temporarily became



```csharp
Console.WriteLine(9);
```


and similarly when executing



```csharp
Console.WriteLine(F(3) + F(4));
```


the program first evaluates F(3) and effectively replaces the
call by the returned result, 9, as if the statement temporarily
became



```csharp
Console.WriteLine(9 + F(4));
```


and then the program evaluates F(4) and effectively replaces
the call by the returned result, 16, as if the statement
temporarily became



```csharp
Console.WriteLine(9 + 16);
```


resulting finally in 25 being calculated and printed.



The first result is 9; the sum is 25. A mathematical analogy describes how returned values combine, but a C# method may also print or change state. Read its contract rather than assuming all methods behave like pure mathematical functions.

```{figure} ../../figures/method_call_return.svg
:alt: A caller passes digit 4 to num in SquareTheNumber. The returned 16 becomes squaredNum in that caller.

Return to the expression that made this call.
```

| Step in `F(3) + F(4)` | Waiting expression |
| --- | --- |
| Evaluate F(3): x receives 3; return 9 | 9 + F(4) |
| Evaluate F(4): x receives 4; return 16 | 9 + 16 |
| Add the returned values | 25 |

The calls have separate parameter values. The method does not remember the previous x as input for the next call.

## Returned Strings and Formatted Results




```{index} Returned Strings and Formatted Results
```


C# methods can return any type of data, not just numbers, and
there can be any number of statements executed before the return
statement. Read, follow, and run the example program, which has `string` as
`return type`:



using System;
Console.WriteLine(LastFirst("Benjamin", "Franklin"));
Console.WriteLine(LastFirst("Andrew", "Harrington"));
static string LastFirst(string firstName, string lastName)
{
    string separator = ", ";
    string result = lastName + separator + firstName;
    return result;
}

The following original trace describes the explicit Main version just above. The top-level runnable version makes the same two calls and receives the same returned strings. First follow the completed trace; then match its steps to source lines as guided practice.


Trace the two complete calls in this worked example.

It is common to want to construct and immediately print a string,
so having `Console.Write` is definitely handy when we want it.
However, sometimes we just want to have the resulting string returned,
so that we can do something else with it. We can use
the C# library method `string.Format`, which does just what we want:
The parameters have the same form as for `Console.Write`,
but the formatted string is *returned*.




Note: The only caveat with `string.Format` is that
there is *no* special method corresponding to `Console.WriteLine`,
with an automatic terminating newline.
You can generate a newline with string.Format: Remember the
escape code `"\n"`. Put it at the end to go on to a new line.



using System;
string saved = SumProblemString(2, 3);
Console.WriteLine(saved);
Console.WriteLine(SumProblemString(12345, 53579));
static string SumProblemString(int x, int y)
{
    int sum = x + y;
    return string.Format("The sum of {0} and {1} is {2}.", x, y, sum);
}


The returned string can be saved before it is printed. `{0}`, `{1}`, and `{2}` in `string.Format` select the following argument values by position. General syntax is `string.Format(formatText, value0, value1, ...)`; interpolation is another formatting form already used in earlier chapters. Neither form prints by itself.

## Print or Return? Choose the Contract




```{index} Print or Return? Choose the Contract
```


using System;
PrintTotal(10m, 2m);
decimal savedTotal = CalculateTotal(10m, 2m);
Console.WriteLine($"Saved plus delivery: {savedTotal + 3m:F2}");
static void PrintTotal(decimal price, decimal charge)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Total: {price + charge:F2}");
}
static decimal CalculateTotal(decimal price, decimal charge)
{
    return price + charge;
}


Both helpers calculate 12.00. PrintTotal writes it immediately and returns no value. CalculateTotal prints nothing; the caller stores 12 and uses it in another expression to print 15.00. A void call cannot be assigned to a decimal. Conversely, calling CalculateTotal and discarding its result is legal, but useless here because that method has no other effect.

**Variation:** change the inputs, store the returned total, and use it twice without repeating user input. **Mistake to diagnose:** `decimal total = PrintTotal(10m, 2m);` asks a void method for a value. The compiler rejects it. Keep calculation reusable and let the caller decide how to display it.

## Decisions, Early Returns, and Complete Return Paths




```{index} Decisions, Early Returns, and Complete Return Paths
```


Methods reuse the decisions and loops you already know. A normal path through a value-returning method must return a compatible value; writing one return somewhere is not enough. A return exits the current call immediately. A void method may use `return;` to finish early, but cannot use `return value;`.

The following valid-input contract accepts a nonnegative subtotal, gives free delivery at 50.00 or above, and charges 4.00 otherwise. The tests cover just below, at, and above the boundary.


using System;
Console.WriteLine($"49.99: {DeliveryCharge(49.99m):F2}");
Console.WriteLine($"50.00: {DeliveryCharge(50m):F2}");
Console.WriteLine($"50.01: {DeliveryCharge(50.01m):F2}");
static decimal DeliveryCharge(decimal subtotal)
{
    if (subtotal >= 50m) return 0m;
    return 4m;
}


The outputs are 4.00, 0.00, and 0.00. Without the final return, a smaller subtotal could reach the end without a result. A return followed by more work on that same path makes the later work unreachable. An accidental semicolon after `if (condition);` creates an empty decision body, so the next statement can run unconditionally. Trace the paths rather than indenting by appearance. The restored return-fragment variations in Extra Practice apply these rules.

Inputs outside the stated domain need a separate policy. Chapter 6 develops exception-based contracts; here do not invent behavior for a negative subtotal without revising the requirement.

You can complete the entire activity with the supplied candidate and your own reasoning; no AI account is required.

A packing charge is a fixed handling amount of 4.00 **plus** `subtotal * rate`. Assume nonnegative inputs. A prepared candidate returns only `subtotal * rate`; its explanation says, “The method calculates the packing charge from the supplied order amount and rate.”

Before running, calculate the required charge for a subtotal of 30.00 and a rate of 0.05. Then calculate it for a zero subtotal. Explain which part of the requirement the candidate omits. Revise the method while keeping its name, parameters, and return type.

**Possible AI prompt:** “Explain whether this method implements a fixed handling amount of 4.00 plus subtotal times rate. Trace inputs 30 and 0 with rate 0.05. Do not change the signature.” Do not accept the explanation without checking the two results yourself.


// Exercise: Review a packing charge
using System;

static decimal PackingCharge(decimal subtotal, decimal rate)
{
    // Your code starts here.

// Solution: Review a packing charge
using System;

static decimal PackingCharge(decimal subtotal, decimal rate)
{

}

Console.WriteLine($"Order: {PackingCharge(30m, 0.05m):F2}");
Console.WriteLine($"Zero subtotal: {PackingCharge(0m, 0.05m):F2}");


The required outputs are 5.50 and 4.00. The zero case exposes the missing fixed amount. A signature tells you how to call a method; its contract tells you what it must do. title: Testing, Debugging, and Error Handling
source:
# Testing, Debugging, and Error Handling Programs fail in many ways: invalid input, missing files, incorrect assumptions, and state bugs that only appear in certain cases. This chapter gives you tools for preventing, diagnosing, and testing those failures. - **Input validation**: Checking values before risky operations prevents many avoidable failures. - **Exception handling**: `try`, `catch`, and related constructs let a program respond intentionally to runtime errors. - **Debugging**: Breakpoints, watches, and step-by-step execution help you inspect what a program is actually doing. - **Unit testing**: Small repeatable tests build confidence that code keeps working as it changes. - **Missing input**: Basic null checks distinguish absent input from valid values. Deeper nullable-type and object-contract discussion follows in Chapter 11. As programs grow, correctness depends less on hoping everything works and more on building habits that make errors visible and manageable.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: QqWfw_CFR6Q :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[C# exception handling ⚠️](https://youtube.com/watch?v=QqWfw_CFR6Q)* by Bro Code. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Validate inputs before operations that can fail 2. Handle runtime exceptions intentionally and communicate useful error messages 3. Use debugger tools to inspect program state and execution flow 4. Write small tests that check expected behavior and failure cases 5. Check for missing input before using it

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`6.1. Error Handling and Validation <0601_error_handling>` - {doc}`6.2. Debugging Workflow <0602_debugging_workflow>` - {doc}`6.3. Unit Testing <0603_testing>` - {doc}`6.4. overview:
# Testing, Debugging, and Error Handling

Programs fail in many ways: invalid input, missing files, incorrect assumptions, and state bugs that only appear in certain cases. This chapter gives you tools for preventing, diagnosing, and testing those failures.

- **Input validation**: Checking values before risky operations prevents many avoidable failures.
- **Exception handling**: `try`, `catch`, and related constructs let a program respond intentionally to runtime errors.
- **Debugging**: Breakpoints, watches, and step-by-step execution help you inspect what a program is actually doing.
- **Unit testing**: Small repeatable tests build confidence that code keeps working as it changes.
- **Missing input**: Basic null checks distinguish absent input from valid values. Deeper nullable-type and object-contract discussion follows in Chapter 11.

As programs grow, correctness depends less on hoping everything works and more on building habits that make errors visible and manageable.
