# Debugging Workflow



```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```


```{index} Turn a Symptom into a Reproducible Question
```



```{index} Debug One Familiar Loop from Symptom to Evidence
```

## Debug One Familiar Loop from Symptom to Evidence


Before the retained array and CSV applications, use a calculation that needs only methods, decisions, and loops. A shop awards one credit for each of the first `days` days. With three days, the expected credits are 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. This expectation comes from the problem, not from running the implementation.

The following complete cell deliberately contains a logic defect. It compiles, but the loop stops too soon. A compiler cannot infer that the business rule requires the last day.


using System;
static int Credits(int days)
{
    int total = 0;
    for (int day = 1; day < days; day++) // Intentional defect: excludes the last day.
        total += day;
    return total;
}
Console.WriteLine($"Expected 6; actual {Credits(3)}");


Save this code as the Program.cs of a console project using the Appendix B workflow. Run `dotnet run` to reproduce the failure before starting a debugger. In VS Code, open the folder containing the project, set a breakpoint on `total += day`, and start the C# debugger for that project. The browser cell can demonstrate the result; the editor debugger supplies paused state.

Write the hypothesis: “the loop omits day three.” A breakpoint pauses **before** the marked statement executes. At its first stop, watch `day`, `days`, and `total`. Step Over the update, then continue to the next stop. Use the method's own frame in the Call Stack panel to inspect its local values. The call stack explains who called the method; it is not a list of all previous loop iterations.

| Observation | day | total before addition | total after addition |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| First stopped iteration | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| Second stopped iteration | 2 | 1 | 3 |
| Third iteration required by the contract | 3 | 3 | 6 |

The third row does not occur in the defective run. After the second addition, `day` becomes three and `day < days` is false. This distinguishes a missing iteration from an incorrect addition. If all three additions had occurred, investigate a later overwrite or the printed expression instead of changing the boundary blindly.

Repair only the condition to `day <= days`. Step through the same input again: a stop with day three should now appear. Keep the old input; changing both the data and the program would weaken the evidence.


using System;
static int Credits(int days)
{
    if (days < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(days));
    int total = 0;
    for (int day = 1; day <= days; day++) total += day;
    return total;
}
static void Check(int days, int expected)
{
    int actual = Credits(days);
    Console.WriteLine($"days={days}: expected={expected}, actual={actual}, pass={actual == expected}");
}
Check(0, 0);
Check(1, 1);
Check(3, 6);
Check(4, 10);


```{index} Use a Different Symptom to Challenge the Hypothesis
```

## Use a Different Symptom to Challenge the Hypothesis


The output compares independently derived expectations with actual results. Zero checks that the loop can run no times; one exposes the original omission immediately; three preserves the original failure; four checks another ordinary case. The negative-input guard is a contract improvement, not the cause of the original wrong total. Record those as separate changes when reviewing a repair.

Guided task: suppose a variant returns 7 for three days. Fill a trace with starting total one instead of zero. Does changing `<` to `<=` alone explain or repair that symptom? Then add an intentional `total = day` in place of `total += day`. Predict the output for four days before debugging.

```{dropdown} Compare the defects
Starting at one adds an unwanted extra credit. With the corrected boundary it yields seven for three days. Assignment instead of accumulation discards earlier credits and returns four for four days. The boundary, initialization and update are separate hypotheses. A trace showing state before and after the update distinguishes them.
```

Use the existing array example after Chapter 7 to transfer this workflow to indexed input. Use the CSV exercise after Chapter 9 to investigate field selection and normalization. Their original tasks remain available; they are later applications rather than assumed knowledge for this first debugger investigation.


```{index} Turn a Symptom into a Reproducible Question
```

## Turn a Symptom into a Reproducible Question



A report says that three expense entries, 12, 8 and 5, total 20. Saying that the total is wrong identifies a symptom, but it does not yet locate the defect. First derive the expected total independently: 12 + 8 + 5 is 25. Keep the three inputs fixed. A changing input set makes it difficult to tell whether a code change repaired the problem or merely avoided it.

Suppose the program loops while index is less than the number of entries minus one. The loop body may contain correct addition and still omit the final item. This is why debugging begins with the contract and a concrete failing case rather than rewriting whichever line looks suspicious. At this point, students can use a simple three-value loop; the same workflow later applies to arrays and object state.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


```{index} Test a Hypothesis Against Execution
```



```{index} Test a Hypothesis Against Execution
```

## Test a Hypothesis Against Execution



State a hypothesis before stepping: perhaps the loop visits only two entries. Put a breakpoint before the loop, not after the incorrect report has already been produced. Observe index, the current input, and the accumulated total. Step over the update, then watch the loop condition. In VS Code, a breakpoint pauses execution when the running program reaches that source location; it does not itself execute or repair the line. Step Into follows a call, while Step Over completes that call without opening its internal steps.

| Observation point | Index being processed | Total after the update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First iteration | 0 | 12 |
| Second iteration | 1 | 20 |
| Expected third iteration | 2 | 25 |

If execution never reaches the third row, the evidence supports an iteration-boundary defect. If all three updates occur but the final result is still 20, investigate later reassignment or output instead. A useful observation distinguishes competing explanations. Repeatedly pressing Step without a question can produce many observations without improving understanding.

The call stack tells you how execution reached the paused method. Local variables belong to the current call; selecting another frame can show another call's values. A watch expression is a view of a value, not proof that the value satisfies a business rule. Prefer observations that do not alter program state. A debugging expression that invokes a mutating method can itself change the behavior you are trying to understand.




```{index} Keep Evidence After the Repair
```



```{index} Keep Evidence After the Repair
```

## Keep Evidence After the Repair



After changing the boundary, rerun the exact 12/8/5 case and record expected 25 versus actual 25. Then check no entries, one entry, and a final entry whose omission would be obvious. These checks do not prove every possible input correct, but they defend against the diagnosed class of defect. Keep the failing case as a regression check rather than replacing it with a new convenient example.

Guided variation: the original failing report contains only one expense of 7 and prints zero. Predict what this says about the loop boundary. Then consider a report that prints 14 instead. The first observation suggests a skipped iteration; the second suggests duplicated processing or a different arithmetic/state problem. The workflow should follow the evidence rather than treating every wrong total as the same bug.


Debugging is a repeatable process, not guesswork.

```{index} The Workflow
```



```{index} The Workflow
```

## The Workflow




Use this sequence every time:

1. Reproduce reliably
2. Minimize the failing case
3. Observe state with tools
4. Form a specific hypothesis
5. Patch one thing
6. Re-test and check for regressions

```{index} Step 1: Reproduce Reliably
```



```{index} Step 1: Reproduce Reliably
```

## Step 1: Reproduce Reliably




Capture:
- exact input
- exact command
- expected behavior
- actual behavior

Without reproducibility, debugging quality collapses.

```{index} Step 2: Minimize the Failing Case
```



```{index} Step 2: Minimize the Failing Case
```

## Step 2: Minimize the Failing Case




Start with a *buggy* example — an off-by-one error in a sum loop:

// Buggy: skips the last element
int[] scores = { 85, 92, 78, 90, 88 };
int total = 0;

for (int i = 0; i < scores.Length - 1; i++)  // BUG: should be <= or just <
    total += scores[i];

Console.WriteLine($"Total: {total}");    // prints 345 instead of 433
Console.WriteLine($"Count: {scores.Length}");

Fix: change the loop condition to `i < scores.Length`:

int[] scores = { 85, 92, 78, 90, 88 };
int total = 0;

for (int i = 0; i < scores.Length; i++)
    total += scores[i];

Console.WriteLine($"Total: {total}");   // 433
Console.WriteLine($"Average: {total / (double)scores.Length:F1}");  // 86.6

```{index} Step 3: Breakpoints and Stepping in VS Code
```



```{index} Step 3: Breakpoints and Stepping in VS Code
```

## Step 3: Breakpoints and Stepping in VS Code




- Set a breakpoint **before** the suspected line
- **Step Over** (`F10`) — execute one line, staying in current method
- **Step Into** (`F11`) — follow execution into a called method
- **Step Out** (`Shift+F11`) — exit the current method

Set the breakpoint on the `total += scores[i]` line and watch `total` after each iteration.

```{index} Step 4: Watch and Call Stack
```



```{index} Step 4: Watch and Call Stack
```

## Step 4: Watch and Call Stack




Inspect:
- key variables before and after transformations
- the call stack to confirm control flow assumptions
- branch conditions at decision points (`if`, loop bounds)

Add a **Watch** expression for `scores[i]` and `total` to see each step.

```{index} Step 5: Typical Bug Patterns
```



```{index} Step 5: Typical Bug Patterns
```

## Step 5: Typical Bug Patterns




| Pattern | Example |
|---------|--------|
| Off-by-one | `i < Length - 1` instead of `i < Length` |
| Stale loop state | reusing a variable without resetting it |
| Null/empty assumption | skipping `IsNullOrWhiteSpace` check |
| Parsing without validation | `int.Parse` on unvalidated input |

```{index} Step 6: Validate the Fix
```



```{index} Step 6: Validate the Fix
```

## Step 6: Validate the Fix




After patching:
1. Re-run the **original** failing input
2. Run edge cases (empty array, single element, max values)
3. Run unit tests if they exist

// Edge case: single element
int[] single = { 42 };
int t = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < single.Length; i++) t += single[i];
Console.WriteLine(t);  // 42

// Edge case: empty array
int[] empty = {};
int t2 = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < empty.Length; i++) t2 += empty[i];
Console.WriteLine(t2);  // 0

```{index} Practice
```

## Practice




Take a method that parses a CSV line:

1. Add one intentional bug (wrong field index, missing `Trim`)
2. Set a breakpoint at the parse start
3. Add a watch on `parts.Length` and each field
4. Step through `TryParse` calls
5. Identify the bug and fix it
6. Re-run with both valid and malformed input

```{rubric} Footnotes
```


[^development-reading]: Further reading: [Microsoft, C# Debugging in VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/csharp/debugging). The worked business scenarios and guided reasoning here are original teaching examples.

# Computing and Society

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

Optional cases extend Chapter 1.2 with software failures, boundary tests, and professional accountability. Use these after the core testing lesson.


Software now sits between people and many things that matter to them: pay, prices, credit, medical treatment, and access to services. The people affected usually never see the code and cannot check it. That gap is why computing professionals carry special responsibility for what their programs do.

```{index} software failures; case studies
```



```{index} When Software Fails People
```

## When Software Fails People



Three well-documented cases show different ways software harms people.

- **Therac-25 (1985–1987).** A radiation therapy machine delivered massive overdoses in six known accidents, killing or seriously injuring patients. Investigators found software race conditions, combined with the removal of hardware safety interlocks that earlier models had relied on and weak engineering practices.[^0605_software_responsibility-therac]
- **Knight Capital (2012).** On August 1, 2012, a trading firm deployed new code to seven of its eight order servers. On the eighth, old, unused code was reactivated. In about 45 minutes it sent millions of unintended orders, and the firm lost more than \$460 million. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission later settled charges with Knight, which paid a \$12 million penalty.[^0605_software_responsibility-knight]
- **The UK Post Office Horizon scandal (1999–2015).** Hundreds of subpostmasters, who run local post offices, were prosecuted for shortfalls that the Horizon accounting system reported. The Post Office itself brought about 700 of these prosecutions. The system had bugs, and the people accused could not see or challenge how it worked. Parliament passed the *Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024* to quash the convictions.[^0605_software_responsibility-horizon]

The lessons differ. Therac-25 shows that removing a safety check because "the software handles it" can be deadly. Knight Capital shows that deployment is part of software quality. Horizon shows the harm done when an organization trusts a system's output over the people it affects.

```{index} defect; scale of impact
```



```{index} Small Defects at Scale
```

## Small Defects at Scale



A defect that costs one customer a few dollars can cost customers in total a great deal, because a program repeats the same mistake every time it runs. The discount rule below is meant to give 10% off orders of \$100.00 or more, but the condition uses `>` instead of `>=`:

using System;

// Intended business rule: orders of $100.00 or more get 10% off.
static decimal DiscountRate(decimal orderTotal)
{
    if (orderTotal > 100.00m)   // defect: should be >=
    {
        return 0.10m;
    }
    return 0.00m;
}

decimal orderTotal = 100.00m;
decimal overcharge = orderTotal * 0.10m - orderTotal * DiscountRate(orderTotal);
Console.WriteLine($"Overcharge on one $100.00 order: ${overcharge:F2}");

// The same small defect, repeated across a year of orders at exactly $100.00
int ordersPerDay = 25;
int ordersAtThreshold = ordersPerDay * 365;
Console.WriteLine($"Orders affected in a year: {ordersAtThreshold}");
Console.WriteLine($"Customers overcharged in total: ${overcharge * ordersAtThreshold:F2}");

No single customer is likely to notice ten dollars, so the defect could run for months. This is exactly the kind of boundary error that the tests in Chapter 6 are designed to catch. Testing the values just below, at, and just above a boundary finds it:

using System;

static decimal DiscountRate(decimal orderTotal)
{
    if (orderTotal >= 100.00m)   // fixed: the boundary value now qualifies
    {
        return 0.10m;
    }
    return 0.00m;
}

// Boundary tests: just below, exactly at, and just above the threshold
Console.WriteLine(DiscountRate(99.99m) == 0.00m ? "PASS 99.99" : "FAIL 99.99");
Console.WriteLine(DiscountRate(100.00m) == 0.10m ? "PASS 100.00" : "FAIL 100.00");
Console.WriteLine(DiscountRate(100.01m) == 0.10m ? "PASS 100.01" : "FAIL 100.01");

Fixing the code is only part of the response. The company must also decide what it owes the customers who were already overcharged. That is an ethical question, not a technical one.

```{index} ethical analysis; checklist
```



```{index} Thinking Through an Ethical Question
```

## Thinking Through an Ethical Question



Ethical decisions in software are rarely about villains. They are usually about trade-offs under deadline pressure. A short checklist keeps the important questions from being skipped:

1. **Who is affected?** List the stakeholders: users, customers, coworkers, the organization, and people outside it.
2. **What could happen, and how bad would it be?** Consider likely and severe outcomes for each stakeholder.
3. **What do we owe them?** Consider laws, contracts, promises made to customers, and professional codes.
4. **Could we explain this decision publicly?** If a decision only works while nobody knows about it, reconsider it.

Applied to the discount defect:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Who is affected? | 9,125 customers who were overcharged; the company; the developer who must report the defect |
| What could happen? | Customers lose \$91,250 in total; if it comes out later, the company loses trust and may face legal action |
| What do we owe them? | The price the company advertised; honest disclosure; a fix that is tested |
| Could we explain it publicly? | "We found an error, fixed it, and refunded everyone" can be explained. "We fixed it quietly and kept the money" cannot. |

```{index} ACM Code of Ethics
```



```{index} Professional Codes of Ethics
```

## Professional Codes of Ethics



Professions write down what they expect of their members. The *ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct*, adopted in 2018 by the largest computing society, is the standard reference for computing.[^0605_software_responsibility-acm] A few of its principles apply directly to the work in this book:

| Principle | What it means for a programmer |
|---|---|
| 1.2 Avoid harm. | Consider who could be hurt by a feature or a failure before you ship it. |
| 1.3 Be honest and trustworthy. | Report defects and limitations, including your own. |
| 1.6 Respect privacy. | Collect and use personal data only for legitimate, stated purposes. |
| 2.1 Strive to achieve high quality in both the processes and products of professional work. | Test, review, and document, as in Chapter 6. |
| 2.5 Give comprehensive and thorough evaluations of computer systems and their impacts, including analysis of possible risks. | Say what could go wrong, not only what works. |
| 2.9 Design and implement systems that are robustly and usably secure. | Build in security from the start, as in the next section. |

```{index} ethics; summary
```



```{index} Summary
```

## Summary



Software affects people who cannot see or check it. Small defects multiply at scale, so testing boundaries is an ethical habit as well as a technical one. When a decision affects others, work through who is affected, what could happen, what is owed, and whether the decision could be explained publicly. Professional codes such as the ACM Code describe what others are entitled to expect from you.

```{rubric} Footnotes
```


[^0605_software_responsibility-therac]: Nancy G. Leveson and Clark S. Turner (1993). An investigation of the Therac-25 accidents. *IEEE Computer*, 26(7), 18–41. <https://web.mit.edu/6.033/2004/wwwdocs/papers/Therac_1.html>

[^0605_software_responsibility-knight]: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (2013). *In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC*, Release No. 34-70694, October 16, 2013. <https://www.sec.gov/litigation/admin/2013/34-70694.pdf>

[^0605_software_responsibility-horizon]: UK Parliament (2024). *Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024*, c. 14. <https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2024/14/contents>; UK Government (2024). *Post Office Horizon convictions quashed*. <https://www.gov.uk/government/news/post-office-horizon-convictions-quashed>

[^0605_software_responsibility-acm]: ACM (2018). *ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct*. <https://www.acm.org/code-of-ethics>

```{index} array type; array ``` (array)= # Arrays An **array is a collection type**: it groups a fixed number of elements of one type and lets the program access them by position. A collection is the broader idea of grouping values and providing operations for working with them. Arrays are the first collection family we study in detail. This chapter covers one-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays, including declaration, initialization, traversal, and method use. - **Array**: An array stores a fixed number of same-typed values under one name. - **Index**: An index selects a specific element by position. - **Traversal**: Loops let a program visit each array element systematically. - **Two-dimensional array**: A 2D array models grid-like data such as tables, boards, and matrices. Arrays establish the ideas of elements, access, traversal, and collection size. A fixed length does not mean fixed contents: you can replace an element without changing the number of positions. Chapter 8, {doc}`Data Collections <../08_collections/0800_data_collections>`, places arrays alongside lists, dictionaries, sets, and collections with specialized processing orders. We study arrays separately here to develop indexing and traversal before comparing those choices.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: IHMmPVEOT64 :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[C# arrays 🚗](https://youtube.com/watch?v=IHMmPVEOT64)* by Bro Code. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Explain why an array is a collection, then declare, initialize, and access one-dimensional arrays 2. Traverse arrays with `for` and `foreach` loops 3. Use array indices safely and explain valid index ranges 4. Declare and process two-dimensional rectangular arrays 5. Pass arrays to methods and return arrays as results

content.chapters/07_arrays/0701_onedim: (one-dim-arrays)= # Creating and Accessing Arrays ```{contents} :local: :depth: 2 ``` ```{index} array; one dimensional ``` ```{index} See the Collection Before Writing Its Loop ``` ## See the Collection Before Writing Its Loop A store records quantities for four delivery slots. Four unrelated variables would require four separate names and repeated processing code. An array gives the values one name and a position-based organization. Its length is fixed when the array object is created; its elements can still change. This connects the collection idea to variables: assignment changes a value in a particular slot, while a loop chooses which slot to visit. Use these schematic forms to distinguish three actions: ```text elementType[] name; // Declare a variable for an array reference. name = new elementType[lengthExpression]; // Create an array and store its reference. name[indexExpression] = valueExpression; // Replace one element of that array. ``` `[]` after the type describes the array type. Brackets after a variable name select an element. Length counts elements; an index identifies a position. For four slots, the valid indexes are zero through three. Index four is already outside the array. using System; int[] quantities = new int[4]; Console.WriteLine($"Before: {string.Join(", ", quantities)}"); quantities[0] = 7; quantities[1] = 5; quantities[2] = 9; quantities[3] = 6; quantities[2] = 4 * quantities[1] - quantities[3]; for (int index = 0; index < quantities.Length; index++) Console.WriteLine($"Slot {index}: {quantities[index]}"); The first line shows default values after allocation. The later assignment reads indexes one and three, computes `4 * 5 - 6`, and stores 14 at index two. It does not insert a fifth quantity or change the array's length. | Index | After allocation | After four assignments | After the calculation | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 0 | 0 | 7 | 7 | | 1 | 0 | 5 | 5 | | 2 | 0 | 9 | 14 | | 3 | 0 | 6 | 6 | Read the table by column to see a whole array state, or by row to follow one element. The loop's condition checks `index < quantities.Length` before each read. The semicolons in a for header separate initialization, condition and update. A comma between condition and update is not the syntax for this loop. An initializer such as `int[] quantities = { 7, 5, 9, 6 };` creates the same four initial values more compactly. Use `foreach` when only the values matter; use an index when the task selects or changes positions. A foreach loop can stop early with `break`, but it does not directly provide the current position for an indexed update. ```{index} Guide a Last-Element Check ``` ## Guide a Last-Element Check An empty array has a real object and Length zero, but it has no last element. A variable containing null has no array object at all. First practice the empty-array distinction; Chapter 11 develops missing references further. Guided task: complete this schematic condition before reading the final element. Explain why `Length - 1` belongs in the index expression, not in the loop's upper bound when all elements are required. ```text if (values.Length /* comparison */ 0) display values[values.Length - 1]; else display "No deliveries"; ``` Predict both calls in the completed example, then change the ordinary input to a one-element array. using System; static void ShowLast(int[] values) { if (values.Length > 0) Console.WriteLine($"Last: {values[values.Length - 1]}"); else Console.WriteLine("No deliveries"); } ShowLast(new int[] { 7, 5, 9, 6 }); ShowLast(Array.Empty()); The comparison is `>`. For an empty array, evaluating index -1 would be invalid, so the read occurs only inside the guarded branch. For one element, Length is one and its last index is zero. As a variation, change only the second slot in the four-element example and predict the entire new state before running it. The retained examples below add other loop forms, string arrays, returned arrays, defaults and library operations. ```{index} 1D Arrays ``` ```{index} array; [ ] declaration ``` An array is a **collection type** and a `data structure` that contains a number of variables that are accessed through computed indices. The variables contained in an array, also called the `elements` of the array, are all of the same type, and this type is called the `element type` of the array. [1] In C#, an array is a structure representing a **fixed length** `ordered` collection of values or objects with the **same type**. Arrays make it easier to organize and operate on large amounts of data. For example, rather than creating 100 integer variables, you can just create one array that stores all those integers and access them using array indices. [2] You have learned that a string is an immutable `sequence` of characters and how to loop through the sequence. Arrays provide more general sequences, with the same indexing notation, but with free choice of the `type` of the items in the sequence, and the ability to `change` the elements in the sequence. The collection idea connects this chapter to the next one. An array supplies an ordered group of elements, indexed access, and traversal, but its length stays fixed after creation. A `List` supports a changing number of elements; a dictionary retrieves values by key; a set represents distinct values; and stacks, queues, and priority queues select the next item by a processing rule. You do not need their syntax yet. First learn the array operations here, then compare the broader families in {doc}`Data Collections <../08_collections/0801_collections>`. The separate chapters mark a learning sequence, not a boundary between arrays and collections. ```{index} Creating Arrays ``` ```{index} Creating Arrays ``` ## Creating Arrays A C# `array variable` is declared similarly to a non-array variable, with the addition of square brackets (`[]`) after the `type` specifier to denote it as an array. So, the general form for declaring an array variable of the element type is: > **type**`[]` variableName; For example, if you want to create an array called `a` with the type `int` for elements, you declare the array variable as: int[] a; In this declaration, you do *not* know how many elements will be in this array from the preceding declaration. You must give further information to create the corresponding `array object`. A new object can be created using the `new` syntax. An array must get a definite length, which can be a literal integer or any integer expression. The general syntax to create a new array is > `new` **type**`[` *length* `]` After the type, there are square brackets enclosing an expression for the length of the array - this length is unchangeable after creation. For example int[] a; a = new int[4]; or, you may combine with the declaration, int[] a = new int[4]; to creates an array that holds 4 integers. After specifying the number of the elements of the array, the default initial values are also assigned. For example, numerical arrays get initialized to all 0’s (false for boolean, the character with Unicode number zero for char, and null for objects and string) with this syntax by default, so when you loop through the array variable: > foreach (int i in a) { Console.Write(i); } 0000 > An **array initializer** consists of a sequence of variable initializers, enclosed by “`{`” and”`}`” tokens and separated by “`,`” tokens. An array initializer can be used in a variable declaration: int[] a = {0, 2, 4, 6, 8}; which is a shorthand for the equivalent `array creation expression`: int[] a = new int[] {0, 2, 4, 6, 8}; Note that the actual data for an array is *not* stored directly in the memory location allocated by the declaration. The array could have any number of items, and hence the memory requirements are not known at compile time. Like all other object (as opposed to primitive) types, what is actually stored at the memory location declared for `a` is a *reference* to the actual place where the data for the array is stored. In actual compiler implementation, this reference is an address in memory. In the diagram below, you see the object references with an arrow *pointing* to the actual location for the object’s data after `a` is initialized: ```{figure} ../../figures/newArray1.png :alt: new array :width: 300px New array. ``` The small box beside `a` is meant to indicate the memory space allocated when `a` is declared. As you can see that space does not actually contain the array, but rather a *reference* to the array, pointing to the actual sequence of data for the array. Also, in the diagram you see the indices associated with each element, though they are not actual a part of what is stored in memory. ```{index} Accessing Array Elements ``` ## Accessing Array Elements ```{index} array; indexing ``` The elements inside an array can to referenced with the same index notation used earlier for strings. a[2] refers to the element at index 2 (third element because of 0 based indexing). Unlike with strings, this element can not only be read, but also be assigned to: a[0] = 7; a[1] = 5; a[2] = 9; a[3] = 6; These four assignment statements would replace the original 0 values for each element in the array. This is a verbose way to specify all array values. An array with the same final data could be created with the single declaration: int[] b = {7, 5, 9, 6}; ```{figure} ../../figures/newArray2.png :alt: new array initialized with braces :width: 300px New array initialized with braces. ``` The list in braces ONLY is allowed as an initialization of a variable in a *declaration*, not in a later assignment statement. Technically it is an initializer, not an array literal. Individual array elements can *both* be used in expressions, and be assigned to. Continuing with the earlier example code: a[2] = 4*a[1] - a[3]; `a[2]` now equals 4\*5 - 6 = 14. Arrays, like strings, have a `Length` property: Console.WriteLine(b.Length); // prints 4 just like with strings. In practice array elements are almost always referred to with an index variable. A very common pattern is to deal with each element in sequence, and the syntax is the same as for a string. Print all elements of array `b`: for (int i= 0; i < b.Length; i++) { Console.WriteLine(b[i]); } The `foreach` syntax would be: foreach ( int x in b) { Console.WriteLine(x); } while the `while` loop syntax would be: > int[] a = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }; > int i = 0; > while ( i < a.Length){ Console.Write(a[i]); i++; } 12345 > In the `foreach` loop, the `int` type for `x` matches the element type of the array `b`. The shorter `foreach` syntax is not as general as the `for` syntax. For example, to print only the first *3* elements of b: for(int i= 0; i < 3; i++) { Console.WriteLine(b[i]); } a plain `foreach` visits the sequence values without exposing an index. It can stop early with `break`, but an indexed loop expresses this position-based limit directly. Also, you may use the `for` syntax to assign new values to the array elements, rather than just use the values in expressions: for(int i= 0; i < b.Length; i++) { b[i] = 5*i; } Now the array `b` of our earlier examples (of length 4) would now contain 0, 5, 10, and 15. There is no analog of *changing* the value of `b[i]` with a `foreach` loop. To change values in an array, we must assign to each location in the array by *index*. A `foreach` loop only provides the *value* of each sequence element for us to read. We have had the array indices so far be given by a single symbol, which is the most common case in practice, but in fact what appears inside the square braces can be any `int` *expression*. Like parentheses, square brackets *delimit* the inside expression, which gets evaluated first, before the array value is looked up. Consider this runnable C# sequence: ``` none > int[] a = {5, 9, 15, -4}; > int i = 2; > a[i]; 15 ``` This should be clear. Now think first, what should `a[i+1]` be? ``` none > a[i+1]; -4 ``` In steps: `a[i+1]` is `a[2+1]` is `a[3]` is -4. Be careful, `a[i+1]` is *NOT* `a[i] + 1` (which would be 16). ```{index} array; as parameter ``` (printstrings)= The code above to print each element of an array performs a unified and possibly useful operation, so it would make sense to encapsulate it into a function. A function can take any type as a parameter, so an array type is perfectly reasonable! Above we printed each element of an array of integers. This time let’s choose strings, so the formal parameter is an array of strings: `string[]`. ```{code-block} csharp :linenos: /// Print the strings in data, one per line. public static void PrintStrings(string[] data) { foreach( string s in data) { Console.WriteLine(s); } } ``` With this definition, the code fragment string[] hamlet = {"To be", "or not", "to be!"}; PrintStrings(hamlet); would print: ``` none To be or not to be! ``` Here we are just reading the data from the array parameter. We will see that there are more wrinkles to array parameters in {ref}`alias`. ```{index} function; return array ``` An array type can also be returned like any other type. Examine the function definition: ```csharp /// Return an array with string data obtained from the user. /// The length of the array and the number of entries to /// prompt the user for is n. public static string[] InputNStrings(int n) { string[] lines = new string[n]; Console.WriteLine ("Enter {0} string(s).", n); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { Console.Write("next string: "); lines[i] = Console.ReadLine(); } return lines; } ``` This code follows a standard pattern for functions returning an array: - In order to return an array, we must *first create* a new array with the `new` syntax. We must set the proper length (`n` here). - And we are not done with one line of creation: Since the array has multiple parts, we need a loop to assign all the values. We have a simple `for` loop to assign to each element in turn. - Finally we must return the array that we created! ```{index} OOP; default value ``` ```{index} Default Initializations ``` ```{index} Default Initializations ``` (default-fields)= ## Default Initializations Did you notice that when the first example array of integers was created, it was filled with zeros? It is a safety feature of C# that the internal fields of objects always get a specific value, not random data. Here are the defaults: | Type | Default element value | | --- | --- | | Primitive numeric types | 0 | | bool | false | | Reference types, including string | null | ```{warning} An array with elements of reference type, like `string[]`, without a specific initializer gets initialized to all null values. Array creation is legal, but reading a member of a null element fails. ``` This intentionally failing fragment illustrates the missing-element problem: ```csharp string[] words = new string[10]; Console.WriteLine(words[0].Length); // Runtime error: this element is null. ``` The error is because null is not an object and has no Length property. If you want an array of empty strings, initialize the elements with a loop: ```csharp string[] words = new string[10]; for (int i = 0; i < words.Length; i++) { words[i] = ""; } ``` ```{index} LINQ Methods ``` ## LINQ Methods Language-Integrated Query (LINQ) is a set of technologies integrating query capabilities into C#. The full query topic is later reading; these calls are library aggregation examples. All C# array types derive from System.Array. Arrays provide enumeration, which permits LINQ extension calls such as Max(), Min(), Sum() and Reverse() when the appropriate namespace is imported. Reverse() produces a sequence rather than automatically changing the original array. ```csharp using System.Linq; int[] nums = new int[5] { 10, 15, 16, 8, 6 }; nums.Max(); // Returns 16. nums.Min(); // Returns 6. nums.Sum(); // Returns 55. nums.Average(); // Returns 11. ``` The average is 55 divided by five. These fragments illustrate result values; they do not print them. The complete runnable examples earlier show how to display results. **Check the library-method summary:** The five values 10, 15, 16, 8 and 6 have sum 55, so their average is 55 / 5 = 11. The Average result comment above is corrected to 11. Sum and Average are different aggregation contracts, even when both consume the same values. The array-processing lesson supplies complete runnable loop examples. The array declarations and initialization forms above follow these references.[^arrays-specification][^arrays-cheatsheet] ```{rubric} Footnotes ``` [^arrays-specification]: See [Arrays](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/arrays) in the Microsoft language specification. [^arrays-cheatsheet]: See the [C# arrays cheatsheet](https://www.codecademy.com/learn/learn-c-sharp/modules/learn-csharp-arrays/cheatsheet) from Codecademy.

## Process Positions Before Introducing a New Container



An array gives many values one shared organization. To calculate a total, the program still needs a rule for visiting those values and combining them. The accumulator pattern connects arrays to Chapter 4: initialize a running result, visit each relevant element, and update the result exactly once for that element. The array changes where input values come from; it does not change the meaning of a loop or an assignment.

Suppose daily quantities are 4, 0 and 7. Before the first iteration the total is zero because no entries have been processed. After each iteration, total should equal the sum of the processed prefix. This claim explains both the initialization and the update. It also provides a way to find a defect before the final result is printed.

| Processed positions | Next position | Total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| None | 0 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | 4 |
| 0 and 1 | 2 | 4 |
| 0 through 2 | End | 11 |

A for loop exposes positions and is useful when you must report an index or replace elements. A foreach loop exposes each element value directly and is useful when only those values matter. Do not assume that changing a foreach iteration variable updates an array element. Use explicit indexing when the operation is defined in terms of changing positions.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


```{index} Passing an Array Does Not Copy Its Elements
```



```{index} Passing an Array Does Not Copy Its Elements
```

## Passing an Array Does Not Copy Its Elements



A method parameter of type int[] receives a copy of the reference value. Caller and helper can therefore refer to the same array. Replacing an element through the helper is visible through the caller's reference. Reassigning the helper's parameter to a different array changes that local parameter, not the caller's variable. This connects ordinary parameter passing from Chapter 5 with reference aliasing, without requiring pass-by-reference parameter syntax.

State whether a processing helper may mutate its input. A Total helper normally only reads values. An ApplyAdjustment helper might intentionally replace them. If a reporting task must preserve original values, computing into another array or returning a separate result is a different contract from modifying the original and restoring it afterward.

An empty array is a real collection with Length zero. A total over no quantities naturally returns zero under the sum contract. A request for the first element has no valid result on that same input. Handle the operation's domain rather than giving every array helper the same empty-case behavior. A null reference is different again: there is no array object whose Length can be read.

Guided exercise: replace the quantities with 0, 0 and 7. Predict the accumulator trace. Then predict the result for an empty array. Finally, explain whether the read-only total should change if another variable is assigned the array reference. An alias alone changes no element, but a later mutation through either alias can change what a subsequent total reads.


using System;
int[] quantities = { 4, 0, 7 };
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < quantities.Length; i++)
{
    total += quantities[i];
    Console.WriteLine($"After position {i}: {total}");
}
Console.WriteLine($"Empty total: {Total(Array.Empty<int>())}");
static int Total(int[] values)
{
    int result = 0;
    foreach (int value in values) result += value;
    return result;
}

% String Method Split

% ———————

% A string method producing an array:

% `string[] Split(char` **separator** `)`

% Returns an array of substrings from *this* string. They are the pieces left

% after chopping out the separator character from the string.

% A piece may be the empty string.

% Example:

% .. code-block:: none

% \> var fruitString = “apple pear banana”;

% \> string\[\] fruit = fruitString.Split(’ ’);

% \> fruit;

% { “apple”, “pear”, “banana” }

% \> fruit\[1\];

% “pear”

% \> var s = ” extra spaces “;

% \> s.Split(’ ’);

% { ““,”“,”extra”, ““,”“,”spaces”, “” }

% Note: The response with the list in braces is a purely *csharprepl* convention for displaying

% sequences for the user. There is no corresponding string displayed by C# Write commands.

% Also see that the string is split at *each* `separator`,

% even if that produces empty strings.

% .. index:: IntsFromString1

% index; parallel arrays

% .. \_ints_from_string1:

% `Split` is useful for parsing a line with several parts. You might get a group of

% integers on a line of text, for instance from::

% string input = UI.PromptLine(

% “Please enter some integers, separated by single spaces:”);

% To extract the numbers, you want to the separate the entries in the string

% with `Split`, *and* you probably want further processing:

% If you want them as integers, not strings, you must convert each one separately.

% It is useful to put this idea in a function.

% See the type returned. It is an array `int[]` for the int results::

% /// Return ints taken from space separated integers in a string.

% public static int\[\] IntsFromString1(string input)

% {

% string\[\] integers = input.Split(’ ’);

% int\[\] data = new int\[integers.Length\];

% for (int i=0; i \< data.Length; i++)

% data\[i\] = int.Parse(integers\[i\]);

% return data;

% }

% In a call to `IntsFromString1("2 5 22")`, `integers` would be

% an array containing strings `"2"`, `"5"`, and `"22"`.

% We need the conversions to `int` to go in a new array that we call `data`.

% We must set its length, which will clearly be the same as for `integers`,

% `integers.Length`.

% To assign elements into `data` we need a loop providing indices,

% like the `for` loop provided. Then for each index, we parse a

% string in `integers` into an `int`,

% and place the `int` in the corresponding location in `data`. We need to return

% `data` at the end to make it accessible to the caller.

% Again we use the basic pattern for returning an array.

% Dealing with arrays is hard for many students for several reasons:

% \* You have new array declaration and creation syntax.

% \* Array are compound objects, so there is a lot to think about.

% \* Loops are hard for many people, and you almost always deal with loops.

% \* You usually must deal with index variables, and there are many

% patterns.

% The last point is significant,

% so it is important to note the special pattern in the example above:

% .. note::

% The use of the same index variable for more than one array is

% a standard way to have

% *related* entries in *corresponding* positions in the arrays.

% We will introduce a refinement of this function in the

% :ref:`intsfromstring_exercise`. It will rely on a more complicated

% index-handling pattern.


(alias)=

## References and Aliases




Object variables, like arrays, are references,
and this has important implications for
assignment.

With a primitive type like an `int`, an assignment copies the data:

`{image} ../../figures/intCopy.png :align: center :alt: copying an int :width: 90 pt`

In the diagram, the contents of the memory box labeled `b` is copied to the
memory box labeled `d`. The value of `d` starts off equal to the value of `b`,
but can later be changed independently.

Contrast an assignment with arrays. The value that is copied is the *reference*,
not the array data itself, so both end up pointing at the *same* actual array:

`{image} ../../figures/arrayAlias.png :align: center :alt: copying an array reference :width: 300 pt`

Hereafter, array assignments like:

    b[2] = -10;
    d[1] = 55;

would both change the *same* array. Now `b` and `d` are essentially
names for the same thing (the actual array). The technical term matches English:
The names are *aliases*.

This may seem like a pretty silly discussion. Why bother to give two different
names to the same object? Isn’t one enough? In fact it is very important
in function/method calls. An array reference can be passed as an actual value,
and it is the array *reference* that is copied to the formal parameter, so
the formal parameter name is an **alias** for the actual parameter name.

If an array passed as a parameter to a method has elements changed in the
method, then the change affects the actual parameter array.
The change *remains* in the actual parameter array *after*
the method has terminated.

```{index} array; Scale example
```

For example, consider the following function:

    // Modify a by multiplying all elements by multiplier.
    static void Scale(int[] a, int multiplier)
    {
       for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) {
          a[i] *= multiplier;  // or:  a[i] = a[i] * multiplier
       }
    }

The fragment:

    int[] nums = {2, 4, 1};
    Scale(nums, 5);

would *change* nums, so it ends up containing elements 10, 20, and 5.

content.chapters/08_collections/0801_collections: (collections-section)= # Collection Families and Selection ```{contents} :local: :depth: 2 ``` ```{index} collections ``` ```{index} Data Collections ``` A bookstore handles many groups of values: the quantities sold during a week, the items in a customer's basket, stock quantities indexed by product code, and orders waiting for collection. Each group contains several values, but the program does different work with each one. Finding Tuesday's sales, looking up a product code, and selecting the next order are different questions. The way you organize the values should support the question you need to answer. A **collection** groups values and provides operations for working with them. Arrays are the first collection type we studied: {doc}`Chapter 7 <../07_arrays/0700_arrays>` introduced fixed-length, indexed sequences. Keeping that chapter separate gave us time to practice indexing, traversal, and multidimensional data. It did not put arrays outside the collection category. This chapter broadens our choices to other ready-made collection types in the .NET standard library. These classes are often called **built-in collections** because they come with .NET, although they are library types used by C#, rather than separate C# language features. Arrays have direct C# language syntax, such as `int[]`; collection classes such as `List` are library types. Both belong in our collection-family comparison. This section introduces the big ideas before the detailed syntax: what a collection promises, how values can be accessed, and how to choose among collection families. You will see eight useful families and small demonstrations of their behavior. The next two sections develop `List` and `Dictionary` in depth. For the other families, your goal here is to recognize the need they address and predict their basic behavior, not to memorize every method or implement a data structure. **Reading path:** First explain the access question, compare the families, and connect their operations. Work through arrays/lists, dictionaries, and shared references before the order-summary exercise. Use the linked-list, set, stack/queue, and priority-queue demonstrations to recognize their policies; their implementations and detailed APIs belong to later chapters. The operation tables are references to revisit, not a list of signatures to memorize in one sitting. ```{figure} ../../figures/collection_access_map.svg :alt: Three access questions: a position selects Tuesday in an array, a product key selects stock in a dictionary, and arrival order selects the next service request in a queue. The access question connects the task to a collection family. ``` Read each column from question to collection to operation. The diagram compares access policies, not performance. A program can need several of these policies at once. ```{index} Collections and Operations ``` ## Collections and Operations ```{index} collection; element; collection operation; data structure ``` An **element** is one item stored in a collection. An array of sales quantities has numbers as its elements; a list of product codes has strings. A dictionary stores entries that associate a key with a value. The surrounding collection gives these items an organization and a set of supported actions. Several operations recur across collection families: | Operation | Question it answers | Bookstore example | | --- | --- | --- | | Add or insert | How does a new item enter the group? | Add a product code to the current basket. | | Retrieve | How do you obtain a particular item? | Find the stock quantity associated with a product code. | | Update | How does stored information change? | Replace a recorded quantity after a stock check. | | Remove | How does an item leave the group? | Remove a canceled item from a basket. | | Membership test | Is this item or key present? | Check whether a customer has already used a promotion. | | Traverse | How do you visit the stored items? | Print every item on an order. | | Inspect size | How many items are stored? | Count the orders waiting for collection. | Not every collection offers every operation, and the method names differ. A stack deliberately limits which item you retrieve next. An array lets you replace an element but does not let you add a new position to that same array. The operations and their rules form a collection's **contract**: the behavior a programmer can rely on. A **data structure** is an organization of stored information that supports operations. A library collection gives you an already implemented data structure through a public interface of methods and properties. You can use a list before you know how its storage grows, just as you can call `Math.Round` before implementing a rounding algorithm. Later chapters examine the implementation choices behind these operations. Keep the question of behavior separate from the question of storage. A queue promises a first-in, first-out processing rule. That rule does not require you to know whether a particular implementation uses an array or linked nodes. Conversely, the fact that two collections both store strings does not mean that their access rules are interchangeable. ```{index} Collection Families ``` (collections-by-access-pattern)= ## Collection Families ```{index} collection; families; access pattern ``` An **access pattern** describes how a program usually retrieves and processes its data. Do you know an item's position? Do you know a key that identifies it? Do you only need to know whether it is present? Must items be processed in arrival order? In the type names below, `T` stands for an element type you choose, such as `string` or `int`. `TKey`, `TValue`, and `TPriority` name the corresponding key, value, and priority types. The examples later in this section use `new` to construct a collection and dot notation to call its operations. First, read the table for the organizing idea behind each family; the next discussion explains generic type arguments before you examine the individual examples. **Table: An introductory map of .NET collection families.** Adapted from Microsoft's collection-selection guidance, with original business examples and an added priority-queue entry.[^0801_collections-collection-guide][^0801_collections-priority-queue] These eight families are a teaching selection, not Microsoft's exhaustive classification. Sorted variants and collections for specialized settings extend this map. | Family | Representative type | Main access rule | Business use | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Array | `T[]`, such as `int[]` | Retrieve by index; length is fixed. | Store one quantity for each of five business days. | | List | `List` | Retrieve by index; the sequence can grow or shrink. | Build a customer's basket as items are selected. | | Linked list | `LinkedList` | Follow linked nodes; insert or remove at a known node. | Insert a processing step beside an already located step. | | Dictionary | `Dictionary` | Retrieve a value using its unique key. | Look up stock by product code. | | Set | `HashSet` | Test membership; equal values occur only once. | Track distinct customers who used a promotion. | | Stack | `Stack` | Retrieve the most recently added item first. | Keep a history of actions to undo. | | Queue | `Queue` | Retrieve the earliest added item first. | Process service requests in arrival order. | | Priority queue | `PriorityQueue` | Retrieve an item with the lowest priority value first. | Process urgent requests before routine requests. | The same business process can need several collections. A bookstore might use a dictionary for stock lookup, a list for basket contents, and a queue for orders awaiting service. Choosing one collection does not commit the whole application to that family. Three distinctions help you read the table. **Position** identifies where an element currently sits in a sequence. **Identity** identifies which entity you mean, such as a product code. **Processing order** determines which waiting item is handled next. Confusing these ideas produces fragile programs: a product code should not silently change because an earlier item was removed from a list. ```{index} Choosing a Collection ``` ## Choosing a Collection ```{index} collection selection; duplicate; order; lookup ``` Start with the work the program must do, rather than the longest list of available methods. For a bookstore promotion, suppose the manager asks for four results: the order of product selections, the current stock for a known code, the distinct customers who participated, and the next request to process. An ordered list preserves selections, including repeated product codes. A dictionary associates a product code with its stock quantity. A set records distinct participating customers. A queue selects the next request if the policy is arrival order; a priority queue is appropriate if a defined priority rule should determine service. These structures can collaborate in one application because they answer different questions. Use the following questions to explain a choice: 1. **What is one element?** A product code, an integer quantity, or a request is a different unit of information. Define what an entry represents before choosing a type. 2. **How will you retrieve it?** Distinguish an index, an identifying key, a membership test, and a next-item rule. 3. **Do order and duplicates carry information?** Removing duplicates from a transaction history can lose events. Preserving every duplicate in a distinct-customer report can misstate participation. 4. **Does the size change?** Decide whether fixed positions describe the task or whether adding and removing elements is normal work. 5. **What operations must be safe?** Consider missing keys, empty collections, invalid values, and whether another part of the program shares the object. Performance matters too, but "fast" needs an operation and a situation. A dictionary is designed for lookup by key; it does not make every kind of search or report automatically fast. A linked list can insert beside a known node without shifting a suffix, but finding that node can take traversal. Later chapters develop these costs systematically. Here, explain the behavioral fit first and avoid claims that one family is always best. Trees and graphs extend the larger study of data structures. They model hierarchies and networks, rather than adding two more standard generic classes named `Tree` and `Graph` to this table. Chapters 17 and 20 teach those structures and their applications. Arrays are developed in Chapter 7; linked structures in Chapter 14; stacks and queues in Chapter 15; priority queues in Chapter 18; and hashing and sets in Chapter 19. For this chapter's detailed coding and assignments, concentrate on lists and dictionaries. The broader family map should help you recognize alternatives and ask better questions about the data. You do not need the internal mechanics of a hash table or heap to explain why a lookup table and a waiting line have different access rules. **Guided choice: the daily order desk** A shop stores five daily sales totals, receives a changing sequence of basket items, looks up stock by product code, and handles requests in arrival order. For each requirement, name the identifying information (position, key, or processing order), select a family, and explain one unsuitable alternative. Then change the requirement: what if urgent requests should go first? ```{dropdown} Reasoning to compare with yours Five fixed positions fit an array. Basket items fit a list because their number changes and repeated selections can matter. Stock lookup fits a dictionary keyed by product code. Arrival-order service fits a queue; a stack would serve the most recent request first. Urgency suggests a priority queue with an explicitly defined priority policy. These choices follow the operations, not the fact that all four groups contain business data. ``` ```{rubric} Footnotes ``` [^0801_collections-collection-guide]: Microsoft. [*Collections and Data Structures*](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/) and [*Selecting a Collection Class*](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/selecting-a-collection-class). Microsoft Learn. Accessed October 16, 2026. The table adapts the documentation's operation-based selection approach; its eight-family grouping and bookstore examples are the author's teaching organization. The priority-queue entry is additionally supported by the API reference below. [^0801_collections-linked-list]: The .NET [LinkedList reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.linkedlist-1?view=net-10.0) describes its node-based, doubly linked organization. [^0801_collections-priority-queue]: The .NET [PriorityQueue reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.priorityqueue-2?view=net-10.0) specifies lowest-priority removal and does not guarantee FIFO behavior for equal priorities. [^0801_collections-collection-interface]: `IEnumerable` supplies an enumerator used by `foreach`. Enumeration order belongs to each type's contract; supporting enumeration does not imply sorted, insertion, or priority order. [^0801_collections-collection-operations]: Microsoft Learn, .NET 10 API reference: [List](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.list-1?view=net-10.0), [LinkedList](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.linkedlist-1?view=net-10.0), [Dictionary](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.dictionary-2?view=net-10.0), [HashSet](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.hashset-1?view=net-10.0), [Stack](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.stack-1?view=net-10.0), [Queue](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.queue-1?view=net-10.0), and [PriorityQueue](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.priorityqueue-2?view=net-10.0). This table compares selected operations rather than listing each type's complete API.
