```{index} Read an Operation as a State Change and a Result
```

## Read an Operation as a State Change and a Result



The family map tells you which question a collection can answer. Now describe an operation with three parts: what must already be true, what changes, and what result the caller receives. This makes the cross-family tables below more useful than a list of names to memorize.

Consider the sequence of product codes PEN, PAD, PEN. Removing by value selects an occurrence matching a value; removing by index selects a position. Popping a stack or dequeuing a queue selects according to processing order instead. Even when each operation reduces a count by one, it need not select the same element. Compare the selection rule before comparing the method spelling.

| Intended action | Information supplied | Question to ask before calling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remove a known product code from a list | Value | Which matching occurrence is removed? |
| Remove the third list position | Index 2 | Does that position exist now? |
| Take the next queued request | No identifying key | Is the queue nonempty? |
| Find stock for a product code | Key | What happens when that key is absent? |

Returning a value and mutating a collection are independent possibilities. A lookup can return a result without removing anything. A removal can both change storage and report success. A Try-style operation supplies a Boolean success signal so that an absent result can be distinguished from a legitimate default value. Read both the success flag and the output value under the documented contract.

Traversal is also an operation with a contract. Foreach provides a shared language form, but it does not make the collection families share one universal order. A sequence has positional order; a work queue has a service policy; a keyed collection has its own enumeration guarantees. If a report requires sorted product codes, request or construct that order explicitly instead of assuming that lookup storage supplies it.

Guided comparison: there are two PEN entries. Explain how Remove("PEN"), RemoveAt(2), and a queue Dequeue could affect a three-item group differently. Draw the before/after contents and identify the selected item. Then explain why the original array cannot shrink merely because an element has been set to an empty string. Replacing a value is not changing the length of the same array.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


```{index} Generic Collections
```

## Generic Collections




```{index} generic type; type parameter; type argument; type safety
```


A collection's **family** tells you how it organizes access. Its **element type** tells you what values it stores. These are separate choices: a list of integers and a list of strings use the same sequence operations, but they store different kinds of values.

A **generic type** is defined using one or more **type parameters**, which are placeholders for types. In documentation, `List<T>` means a list whose element type is represented by `T`. When you write `List<string>`, `string` is the **type argument** you have supplied for that parameter. The library provides the reusable class; you choose its type arguments when declaring the collection.

| Library notation | Example in a program | Meaning of the type arguments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `List<T>` | `List<string>` | Each element is a string. |
| `HashSet<T>` | `HashSet<int>` | Each distinct element is an integer. |
| `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` | `Dictionary<string, int>` | Keys are strings; values are integers. |
| `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>` | `PriorityQueue<string, int>` | Elements are strings; priorities are integers. |

Generic collections provide **type safety**: the compiler checks whether supplied values can be used as the declared types. A `List<int>` accepts integers; it will not accept the string `"twelve"`. This catches a mismatch before the program runs. It does not establish that every integer is appropriate: a negative stock quantity is still an integer, so business validation remains your responsibility.


```{index} The Standard Library and Namespaces
```

### The Standard Library and Namespaces




```{index} namespace; standard library; System.Collections.Generic
```


A **namespace** groups related type names. Most collection classes demonstrated here belong to `System.Collections.Generic`. The `using System.Collections.Generic;` directive lets you write `List<string>` instead of the full name `System.Collections.Generic.List<string>`. It makes names available; it does not create a collection or download a package.

Creating a collection requires constructing an object, as in `new List<string>()`. The parentheses call a **constructor**, which initializes the new object. You will study constructors and your own class definitions in Chapter 10. For now, you are using classes already supplied by the library, just as earlier examples used library methods.

Some modern C# projects import common namespaces automatically. Every runnable example here includes the imports it needs so you can run it independently. The following diagram shows three collection namespaces you may encounter, rather than a complete inventory of .NET collections.

:::{figure} ../../figures/collection_namespaces.svg
:width: 700

Selected .NET collection namespaces: generic collections, older non-generic collections, and concurrent collections.
:::

Prefer the generic collection classes for new code like the examples in this chapter. Older non-generic types, such as `ArrayList` and `Hashtable`, commonly store values through `object` and do not provide the same element-type checking. Recognizing their names can help you read older programs; learning them is not a separate requirement here.

Other library collections address additional needs. Sorted dictionaries and sorted sets maintain ordering by key or element, rather than merely remembering positions. Concurrent collections support coordinated access from multiple threads. Immutable collections produce updated versions without changing the original collection. These are additional dimensions of collection design, not extra families that you must master in this lesson.


```{index} Similar Operations, Different Methods
```

(collection-operation-syntax)=

## Similar Operations, Different Methods




```{index} collection; operation comparison; method call; property; indexer
```


The families share familiar questions: how do we put an item in, inspect it, take it out, or count the items? Their method names express different rules for answering those questions. Connect each name to the operation you already understand before learning its spelling. This is a comparison map; the worked family examples below and Sections 8.3–8.4 develop the details.[^0801_collections-collection-operations]

The general syntax for calling an instance method is:

```text
collection.MethodName(argument1, argument2, ...);
resultType result = collection.MethodName(arguments);
```

These are syntax patterns, not programs to paste unchanged. `collection` stands for an existing collection variable; the dot selects a member. Replace `MethodName` with the actual name and supply the required arguments inside parentheses. A method with no arguments still needs `()`. Use the second pattern only when the method returns a value you want to store; `resultType` must match that value's type. Some methods change the collection, some return information, and some do both.

Properties and indexers have different syntax:

```text
int size = collection.Count;
elementType item = sequence[index];
valueType value = dictionary[key];
```

`Count` is a property, so it has no parentheses. An array uses `Length` instead. Square brackets select an array/list position or a dictionary key. `elementType` and `valueType` stand for the actual stored types, such as `string` or `int`. An index and a key are different ways to identify an item, even though both use brackets.


```{index} Put In, Inspect, and Take Out
```

### Put In, Inspect, and Take Out




```{index} Add; Remove; RemoveAt; Push; Pop; Peek; Enqueue; Dequeue
```


The following table shows calls on variables named for their collection family. `item`, `key`, `value`, `index`, and `priority` represent values already available to the program. These calls are alternatives for different types, not one interchangeable API.

| Family | Put an item in | Inspect or retrieve | Take an item out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Array, `T[]` | Fill an existing position: `array[index] = item` | `array[index]` | No operation shrinks this same array. |
| List, `List<T>` | `list.Add(item)`; `list.Insert(index, item)` | `list[index]` | `list.Remove(item)`; `list.RemoveAt(index)` |
| Linked list, `LinkedList<T>` | `linked.AddFirst(item)`; `linked.AddLast(item)` | `linked.First.Value` or `linked.Last.Value`, when nonempty | `linked.Remove(item)`; `linked.RemoveFirst()`; `linked.RemoveLast()` |
| Dictionary, `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` | `dictionary.Add(key, value)` | `dictionary[key]`, when the key exists | `dictionary.Remove(key)` |
| Set, `HashSet<T>` | `set.Add(item)` | `set.Contains(item)` tests membership | `set.Remove(item)` |
| Stack, `Stack<T>` | `stack.Push(item)` | `stack.Peek()` inspects the top | `stack.Pop()` removes **and returns** the top |
| Queue, `Queue<T>` | `queue.Enqueue(item)` | `queue.Peek()` inspects the front | `queue.Dequeue()` removes **and returns** the front |
| Priority queue, `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>` | `priorityQueue.Enqueue(item, priority)` | `priorityQueue.Peek()` inspects the next item | `priorityQueue.Dequeue()` removes **and returns** the next item |

`Add`, `Push`, and `Enqueue` all put an item into a collection, but they express different access policies. `Remove`, `Pop`, and `Dequeue` all remove something, but they do not select it in the same way or return the same kind of result. `Peek` reads the next item without removing it. With the default priority comparer, a lower priority value is selected first; equal priorities do not guarantee arrival order.

For a list, `Remove(item)` removes the first equal item and returns a Boolean indicating success. `RemoveAt(index)` removes the item at a position and returns no value. For an integer list, this distinction matters: `Remove(2)` searches for the **value** 2, whereas `RemoveAt(2)` selects the **third position**. A set's `Add` returns `false` for a duplicate. A dictionary's `Add` rejects a duplicate key, while `dictionary[key] = value` inserts a missing key or replaces its current value. Similar names do not guarantee identical behavior.

An array's fixed length is part of its contract. Replacing a slot is an update, not insertion; setting it to zero or null does not remove the slot. Creating another array or using a resizable list is a different operation.


```{index} Size, Membership, and Safe Access
```

### Size, Membership, and Safe Access




```{index} Count; Length; Contains; ContainsKey; TryGetValue; TryPop; TryDequeue
```


| Family | How many items? | Is this item or key present? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Array | `array.Length` | `Array.IndexOf(array, item) >= 0` for a one-dimensional array |
| List | `list.Count` | `list.Contains(item)` |
| Linked list | `linked.Count` | `linked.Contains(item)` |
| Dictionary | `dictionary.Count` | `dictionary.ContainsKey(key)` |
| Set | `set.Count` | `set.Contains(item)` |
| Stack | `stack.Count` | `stack.Contains(item)` |
| Queue | `queue.Count` | `queue.Contains(item)` |
| Priority queue | `priorityQueue.Count` | No direct `Contains` method; searching entries is a separate task. |

A membership test answers whether an item exists, not how quickly the search runs. The family demonstrations explain the different access patterns. `foreach` visits elements across these families, but its traversal order follows each type's contract; enumerating a priority queue is not guaranteed to produce priority order.

Before indexing an array or list, check the valid range. Before reading `linked.First.Value`, check that a first node exists. Before calling `Peek`, `Pop`, or `Dequeue`, consider the empty case. These calls throw when no item is available. The library also offers Boolean-returning alternatives: `TryPeek`, `TryPop` for stacks, and `TryDequeue` for queues. Priority queues offer `TryPeek` and `TryDequeue` with both element and priority outputs. Dictionaries offer `TryGetValue` for a key that might be absent.

Their general pattern is:

```text
if (dictionary.TryGetValue(key, out valueType value))
{
    // Use value only after the lookup succeeds.
}
```

`out` allows the method to supply a value through an argument. Here the Boolean result tells the `if` whether the lookup succeeded. Section 8.4 develops this lookup pattern with runnable examples. You do not need to memorize every `Try` signature now; recognize the shared idea of checking success before using a result.

**Make the connections:** A basket needs to add and remove a chosen item; an undo history needs to remove the most recent action; a service line needs to remove the earliest arrival. Explain why these related needs lead to `Add`/`Remove`, `Push`/`Pop`, and `Enqueue`/`Dequeue`. Then identify which operations change size and which only inspect data. Use the following examples to check your predictions.


```{index} Collection Examples
```

## Collection Examples




```{index} collections; examples
```


You now have the family map, the idea of a collection contract, and a way to explain a choice. The following examples make those ideas concrete. For each one, identify what is stored and predict how the collection retrieves it before running the code. The detailed list and dictionary lessons follow in Sections 8.3 and 8.4.


The next example retains the explicit type names so you can see both choices. It stores employee names in a list and associates names with training scores in a dictionary. The commented line illustrates a type mismatch; leave it commented when running the demonstration.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

List<string> names = new List<string> { "Ana", "Bo" };
Dictionary<string, int> scores = new Dictionary<string, int>
{
    ["Ana"] = 92,
    ["Bo"] = 85
};

Console.WriteLine(names[0]);
Console.WriteLine(scores["Bo"]);
// scores["Ana"] = "ninety-two"; // Expected compile error if uncommented: string is not int.


```{index} Arrays and Lists
```

### Arrays and Lists




```{index} array; list; index; sequence
```


A **sequence** gives its elements positions. In the arrays and lists used here, positions are indexed from zero. Both can contain repeated values. Their order is the order of the sequence, which is not necessarily sorted order.

An array's length remains fixed after creation, but its elements can change. Fixed length does not mean read-only data. A list manages storage as elements are added or removed. Its `Count` reports the number of elements currently in the list; an array uses `Length`.

Read this example as a comparison of behavior. The weekly array still has five positions after a correction. The basket grows when a second item is added, and it retains the order of those additions.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

int[] dailySales = { 12, 9, 15, 8, 11 };
dailySales[1] = 10;

List<string> basket = new List<string> { "NOTEBOOK" };
basket.Add("PEN");

Console.WriteLine($"Business days: {dailySales.Length}");
Console.WriteLine($"Tuesday sales: {dailySales[1]}");
Console.WriteLine($"Basket items: {basket.Count}");
Console.WriteLine($"First item: {basket[0]}");


Use an array when a fixed number of indexed positions expresses the task clearly. Use a list when the sequence changes size during normal work. A list is not automatically the best choice simply because it is more flexible: the fixed five-day structure can make the meaning of the array clear. Likewise, repeatedly replacing arrays just to add another basket item makes ordinary work harder than it needs to be.

**Check Your Understanding:** Does changing Tuesday's quantity require a list? What change to the task would make a list more useful?

```{dropdown} Suggested Answer
No. Replacing an existing array element does not change the array's length. A list becomes more useful if you are collecting an unknown or changing number of daily records, rather than maintaining exactly five positions.
```


```{index} Linked Lists
```

### Linked Lists




```{index} linked list; node
```


A **linked list** organizes a sequence as **nodes**, each holding an element and links to neighboring nodes. .NET's `LinkedList<T>` is doubly linked: a node can refer to both its previous and its next node. You do not use `steps[1]` to retrieve its second element. You traverse the sequence or work with a node reference.[^0801_collections-linked-list]

Imagine a sequence of order-processing steps. After locating the packing step, you discover that a gift-check step belongs immediately after it. In the example below, `AddLast` returns a reference to the new node; `AddAfter` uses that reference to choose an insertion point. `var` asks C# to infer the node variable's type from the returned value.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

LinkedList<string> steps = new LinkedList<string>();
var packingStep = steps.AddLast("Pack order");
steps.AddLast("Dispatch order");
steps.AddAfter(packingStep, "Check gift message");

foreach (string step in steps)
{
    Console.WriteLine(step);
}


The result is still an ordered sequence, but it has different access operations from an indexed list. Inserting beside a node you already hold avoids shifting later elements. Finding that node can still require a search, and nodes have storage overhead. A linked list is therefore not a universal replacement for `List<T>`. Chapter 14 develops these tradeoffs and their implementations.


```{index} Dictionaries
```

### Dictionaries




```{index} dictionary; key; value; key-value pair
```


A **dictionary** associates a **key**, which identifies an entry, with a **value**, which is the information stored for that key. A stock lookup might use a product code as the key and an integer quantity as the value. Unlike a list index, the code expresses identity rather than position.

Keys are unique within a dictionary: one key cannot identify two separate entries. Values do not have to be unique. Two products may have the same stock quantity without being the same product. Here both codes initially map to `12`, and the program retrieves a quantity by code.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

Dictionary<string, int> stock = new Dictionary<string, int>
{
    ["NOTEBOOK"] = 12,
    ["PEN"] = 12
};

Console.WriteLine($"Product codes: {stock.Count}");
Console.WriteLine($"Notebook stock: {stock["NOTEBOOK"]}");


The expression `stock["NOTEBOOK"]` asks for a value associated with a key. It does not ask for the first, second, or alphabetically earliest entry. A dictionary is not an alphabetically sorted list, and you should not make a report depend on its enumeration order. You also need a policy for unknown codes; Section 8.4 teaches safe lookup and the difference between adding an entry and updating one.


```{index} Sets
```

### Sets




```{index} set; membership; uniqueness
```


A **set** stores distinct elements and emphasizes **membership**, meaning whether an element is present. Adding an equal element again does not create another copy. A set therefore answers a different question from a list: "Which customers participated?" rather than "What were all the participation events?"

If a customer uses a promotion twice, a list can record both events, while a set can record that customer's participation once. In this demonstration, `Add` returns `false` for the repeated value because no new element was added. `Contains` asks whether an element is in the set.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

HashSet<string> customers = new HashSet<string>();
customers.Add("C101");
customers.Add("C205");
bool addedAgain = customers.Add("C101");

Console.WriteLine($"Distinct customers: {customers.Count}");
Console.WriteLine($"Added C101 again: {addedAgain}");
Console.WriteLine($"C205 participated: {customers.Contains("C205")}");


A set does not preserve the number of times a value appeared. If you need that number, a dictionary can associate each customer with a count. A `HashSet<T>` also does not promise sorted enumeration. Chapter 19 explains hashing, equality, and set operations; here you only need to recognize the membership and uniqueness contract.

**Check Your Understanding:** A list contains the product codes `PEN`, `PEN`, and `NOTEBOOK`. Would a set be a suitable replacement for the basket? Would it be suitable for the distinct products included in a promotion report?

```{dropdown} Suggested Answer
A set would lose the repeated PEN entry, so it would not preserve a basket that uses repeated entries to represent quantity. It would be suitable for a report asking only which distinct product codes appeared. The choice depends on whether duplicates carry information.
```


```{index} Processing Order
```

(rules-for-processing-work)=

### Processing Order




```{index} processing order; stack; queue; priority queue
```


Sometimes the important question is which item should leave the collection next. A list lets you choose a position, but that freedom puts the responsibility for enforcing the processing rule on your program. A stack or queue expresses a particular rule through its operations.

These structures do not decide an organization's policy for you. If requests should be handled in arrival order, choose a collection that expresses that policy. If urgency should take precedence, make the urgency rule explicit and choose a different structure.


```{index} Stacks and Queues
```

### Stacks and Queues




```{index} last in first out; first in first out; push; pop; enqueue; dequeue
```


A **stack** follows **last in, first out (LIFO)**. `Push` adds an item at the top; `Pop` removes and returns the top item. Think of an undo history: the most recent action should normally be the first action undone. Storing a description of an action is only a demonstration of ordering; a real undo feature also needs a way to reverse that action.

A **queue** follows **first in, first out (FIFO)**. `Enqueue` adds an item at the back; `Dequeue` removes and returns the item at the front. This expresses an arrival-order service line.

Both collections below receive `Order A` followed by `Order B`. Predict which order each returns before running the example.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

Stack<string> recentActions = new Stack<string>();
recentActions.Push("Order A");
recentActions.Push("Order B");

Queue<string> waitingOrders = new Queue<string>();
waitingOrders.Enqueue("Order A");
waitingOrders.Enqueue("Order B");

Console.WriteLine($"Stack returns: {recentActions.Pop()}");
Console.WriteLine($"Queue returns: {waitingOrders.Dequeue()}");
Console.WriteLine($"Actions remaining: {recentActions.Count}");
Console.WriteLine($"Orders remaining: {waitingOrders.Count}");


Removing an item changes the collection: each now has one item left. `Peek` lets you inspect the next item without removing it. Removing from an empty stack or queue requires a separate check or a suitable `Try...` operation; this example establishes that both are nonempty before removal. Chapter 15 develops safe operations and practical applications.

The FIFO rule is an ordering rule, not a complete definition of fairness. For example, an arrival-order queue does not by itself accommodate an urgent safety issue. You still need to decide whether arrival order expresses the policy the task actually requires.


```{index} Priority Queues
```

### Priority Queues




```{index} priority queue; priority
```


A **priority queue** chooses the next item using a priority value rather than its arrival position. In .NET's default `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>`, the item with the **lowest priority value** is removed first. A smaller number therefore means earlier processing in this example. This is a convention you must define for the application, not an automatic interpretation of what "high priority" means.[^0801_collections-priority-queue]

Each insertion supplies two pieces of information: the element to store and its priority. A routine request arrives first, but the urgent request leaves first because its priority value is smaller.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

PriorityQueue<string, int> requests = new PriorityQueue<string, int>();
requests.Enqueue("Routine restock", 3);
requests.Enqueue("Urgent replacement", 1);
requests.Enqueue("Scheduled pickup", 2);

while (requests.Count > 0)
{
    Console.WriteLine(requests.Dequeue());
}


The removed items follow the priority rule even though they arrived in another order. A priority queue does not guarantee FIFO order among items with equal priority. If arrival order must break ties, the application needs an explicit tie-breaking rule. The unique priorities in this example avoid that ambiguity. Chapter 18 develops priorities and heap implementations.

**Check Your Understanding:** Which collection fits each task: undo the latest edit, serve the earliest waiting request, or process the smallest urgency number first?

```{dropdown} Suggested Answer
Use a stack for the latest edit, a queue for arrival-order requests, and a priority queue for the smallest urgency value. All three may store the same element type; the difference is the retrieval rule.
```


```{index} Traversal and Shared References
```

## Traversal and Shared References




```{index} traversal; enumeration; IEnumerable; reference; alias; mutation
```


**Traversal**, also called **enumeration**, means visiting a collection's elements. `foreach` provides familiar syntax for this work, but the order and the kind of element you receive depend on the collection. Arrays and lists follow their sequence order. A dictionary enumerates key/value entries. A set supports enumeration, but its purpose is membership rather than sorted traversal. `PriorityQueue` is a special case: it exposes an `UnorderedItems` view for enumeration instead of supporting `foreach` directly on the queue. That view does not promise priority order; use successive removals when you need that order.

The enumerable collection types demonstrated here implement `IEnumerable<T>`, an interface describing how to enumerate values.[^0801_collections-collection-interface] You do not need to write an interface to use these library collections. Later chapters explain how a type can provide this capability itself. Also distinguish traversal from removal: looping through a queue with `foreach` does not serve and remove its waiting items.

Here a traversal computes a total without changing the stored quantities. The accumulator starts at zero, so an empty list would produce a total of zero.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

List<int> quantities = new List<int> { 2, 1, 3 };
int total = 0;
foreach (int quantity in quantities)
{
    total += quantity;
}

Console.WriteLine($"Entries: {quantities.Count}");
Console.WriteLine($"Total units: {total}");


The mutable library collection classes shown here are **reference types**. A variable refers to a collection object. Assigning that variable to another variable copies the reference, rather than making a second collection. Two names for the same object are **aliases**. Arrays have reference behavior too; this continues the idea introduced in Chapter 7.

Consider a basket shown in two parts of a program. If both variables refer to the same basket, adding an item through one variable is visible through the other. If you need a separate snapshot of a list's elements, you must explicitly create a new collection.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

List<string> basket = new List<string> { "NOTEBOOK" };
List<string> sameBasket = basket;
List<string> snapshot = new List<string>(basket);

sameBasket.Add("PEN");

Console.WriteLine($"Original basket: {basket.Count}");
Console.WriteLine($"Alias: {sameBasket.Count}");
Console.WriteLine($"Snapshot: {snapshot.Count}");


`basket` and `sameBasket` refer to one list containing two strings. `snapshot` is a different list containing the one string that was present when it was created. This is a copy of the elements, not a general promise to duplicate every object an element might refer to. Chapter 11 revisits that distinction with objects and composition.

Mutation means changing an existing object's state, such as adding to a list. Reassigning a variable to a different list is a different action. This distinction matters when collections are passed to methods or shared between parts of a program. An operation can affect more code than the variable name immediately in front of you suggests.

You should also check whether an operation is valid during traversal. In particular, adding or removing list elements inside a `foreach` over that same list invalidates its enumeration. Section 8.3 shows a safe removal pattern. A short loop can still be incorrect if it ignores the collection's operating rules.


**Interactive Exercise: An Order Summary**

A small order contains quantities `2`, `1`, and `3`. The starter stores them in a `List<int>`. Compute the total with `foreach` and store that total under the key `"ORD-101"` in a `Dictionary<string, int>`. Print the entry count and the saved total. Expected output is `Line items: 3` and `Saved total: 6` on separate lines.

After running your code, explain why the quantities form a list and why the saved summary uses a dictionary. Change the list to be empty and predict both results before running it again.


// Exercise: An Order Summary
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

List<int> quantities = new List<int> { 2, 1, 3 };

// TODO: Calculate the total, save it by order code, and print the results.
// Your code starts here.



// Your code ends here.


// Solution
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

List<int> quantities = new List<int> { 2, 1, 3 };
int total = 0;
foreach (int quantity in quantities)
{
    total += quantity;
}
Dictionary<string, int> orderTotals = new Dictionary<string, int>();
orderTotals["ORD-101"] = total;

Console.WriteLine($"Line items: {quantities.Count}");
Console.WriteLine($"Saved total: {orderTotals["ORD-101"]}");


The list stores a sequence of quantities, including any repeated quantities. The dictionary associates an order's identity with its total. With an empty list, the entry count and calculated total are both zero. The dictionary still has one entry because the program saves that zero total under `ORD-101`; no line items is different from no saved summary.


```{index} Summary
```

## Summary



Collections combine stored values with rules for using them. Arrays and lists provide indexed sequences; linked lists organize nodes; dictionaries support key-based lookup; sets emphasize uniqueness and membership; stacks, queues, and priority queues determine what comes next. Generic type arguments specify the types of stored elements, keys, values, or priorities.

Choose the collection by explaining the task's access pattern, ordering, duplicates, and changes in size. Then check the details of its contract. The following sections put that reasoning into practice with lists and dictionaries.

```{index} file ``` (files)= # Files and Text Most useful programs eventually read data from outside the program or write results somewhere durable. This chapter introduces file operations and text processing so you can work with multi-line content and structured records. - **File I/O**: File input and output let a program read stored data and save results. - **Streams**: Streams provide a sequence-oriented way to read from or write to a source. - **Text processing**: Trimming, casing, splitting, and replacing help clean and transform text. - **Structured records**: Delimited text such as CSV stores fields that must be parsed and validated. - **Regular expressions**: Regex patterns describe text shapes for search, validation, and extraction. Reliable text handling turns raw files, exports, logs, and user-entered records into data a program can actually use.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: tApBDuVwCrc :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[Read and Write files in 10 minutes | C#](https://youtube.com/watch?v=tApBDuVwCrc)* by tutorialsEU. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Read text from files and write text output safely 2. Clean text with trimming, casing, splitting, and replacement methods 3. Parse structured text lines into typed values 4. Validate fields before using parsed data 5. Use regular expressions for targeted text search and matching

content.chapters/09_files_text/0901_stream_file: (fileabstraction)= (fio)= # File Foundations: Reading and Writing ```{contents} :local: :depth: 2 ``` ```{index} file; stream abstraction ``` ```{index} Files As Streams ``` In most real world scenarios, especially in business settings, operations carried out with computers and information systems usually involve data processing and may generate new data as a result. To make the data *persistent* past the end of program execution, data are stored in file system or databases (for structured data). Although a database maybe preferred in many cases, there will be times that you need to read and write files for various purposes. A file is a collection of data stored on in a storage device with a name and directory path information. A file is stored in your file system, which is part of the operating system (OS), and the OS therefore has the information about the file and how to access it. ```{index} File Stream ``` ```{index} File Stream ``` ## File Stream In .NET, file and stream I/O (input/output) refers to the transfer of data either to or from a storage medium. The System.IO namespaces contain types that enable reading and writing, both synchronously and asynchronously, on data streams and files, in addition to other file and stream operations. You have already read and written streams of characters to the `Console`. Most of the syntax that we use for files will be very similar, using methods `ReadLine`, `WriteLine`, and `Write` in the same way you used them for the `Console`. When you read/write a file in C# program, the data processed is seen as a **Stream**. A stream is a sequence of bytes of data sent between the destination and the source of the file. Streams are how data is read and written to and from files, networks, and computer memory. For example, printing data using a printer involves sending a sequence of bytes of data to a stream associated with a network port connected to the printer. ```{index} File handling process ``` ```{index} File handling process ``` ### File handling process For file handling operations, there are two obvious streams: 1. The **Input Stream** that is used to read data from a file (read operation). 2. The **Output Stream** that is used to write data into a file (write operation). However, different task processes use different type of streams: text files, binary files, strings, and network communications are some of the examples. The basic stream operations therefore include the following: 1. Creation/Opening 2. Reading 3. Writing 4. Positioning 5. Closing ```{index} The System.IO namespace ``` ```{index} The System.IO namespace ``` ### The `System.IO` namespace Files can be handled very differently by different operating systems, but C# abstracts away the differences and provides stream interfaces between a C# program and files through the `System.IO namespace` ({ref}`namespace `). The System.IO namespace contains the required classes used to handle the input and output streams and provide information about file and directory structure. The [System.IO namespace](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io?view=net-8.0) lists all the classes available for use. The [File class](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io.file?view=net-8.0) is one of the classes that provides static methods for the creation, copying, deletion, moving, and opening of a single file, and aids in the creation of FileStream objects. Classes that are commonly used to for file handling include: - The `FileStream` class - Convenience class: `File` class - Helper class: `StreamWriter` - Helper class: `StreamReader` ```{index} Simple File Handling: File Class ``` ```{index} Simple File Handling: File Class ``` (file-class)= ## Simple File Handling: `File` Class Among the file handling methods is the convenience class `File`, which provides `static methods` for the creation, copying, deletion, moving, and opening of a single file, and aids in the creation of `FileStream` objects. For example, the Create(), WriteAllText, ReadAllText() and File.Exists() can be used to perform basic file operations among other methods: **Methods in File Class** | Method | Description | |--------|-------------| | `AppendText()` | Appends text at the end of an existing file | | `Copy()` | Copies a file | | `Create()` | Creates or overwrites a file | | `Delete()` | Deletes a file | | `Exists()` | Tests whether the file exists | | `ReadAllText()` | Reads the contents of a file | | `Replace()` | Replaces the contents of a file with the contents of another file | | `WriteAllText()` | Creates a new file and writes the contents to it. If the file already exists, it will be overwritten. | Sine class `File` provides `static methods`, we can `call` the methods directly by using the `dot notation` without having to create a new instance of the class. For example, with `File` class, when you want to write some content to a file, you can simply say `File.ReadAllText(string path, string content)` to write the string content to the path file. You can perform tests such as the following in a small VS Code project to get familiar with the methods: 1. Create a file using `File.Create (path)`: // path means filename + the file's directory path > File.Create("MyTest.txt"); 2. Check if a file exists using `File.Exists (path)`: > if (File.Exists("MyTest.txt")) { Console.WriteLine("MyTest.txt exists"); } MyTest.txt exists 3. Write to a file using `File.WriteAllText (path, content)`: > File.WriteAllText("MyTest.txt", "Hello, this is a test."); 4. Read from a file using `File.ReadAllText(path)`: > File.ReadAllText("MyTest.txt"); > Console.WriteLine(File.ReadAllText("MyTest.txt")); Hello, this is a test. > To better organize the tests above, use VS Code and a small console project. You should also use a variable for the filename: using System; using System.IO; namespace IntroCSCS { internal class Ch07File { private static void Main(string[] args) { // create a file string path = "MyTest.txt"; // create the file in this directory // File.Create(path); // let WriteAllText create the file // // File.Create() does not close file; leads to exception // test file existence if (File.Exists(path)) { Console.WriteLine($"The file {path} exists."); } // write to the file string str = "Hello, I know how to writing files."; File.WriteAllText(path, str); // static method WriteAllText() will create the file if not exists // read the file string s = File.ReadAllText(path); // static method ReadAllText() for reading from file Console.WriteLine(s); } } } ```{index} StreamWriter; write and close ``` ```{index} StreamWriter ``` (filewrite)= ## `StreamWriter` The `FileStream` class provides a `stream` of bytes[] of data for file operations, supporting both synchronous and asynchronous read and write operations. To use the FileStream class in C#, first of all, you need to include the `System.IO namespace` and then you need to create an `instance` of the FileStream class in order to use its functionalities to, for example, create a new file or to open an existing file. For handling files, the `StreamWriter` class is more popular in writing files and it is very helpful in writing text data into a file. It is easy to use and provides a complete set of constructors [^0902_file_operations-constructor] and methods to work on it. Specifically, the `StreamWriter` class in C# is used for writing characters to stream in a particular format. ```{index} Writing Files ``` ```{index} Writing Files ``` ## Writing Files Observe the following program (`first_file.cs`): using System; using System.IO; namespace IntroCSCS { class Ch07File // basics of file writing { public static void Main() { StreamWriter writer = new StreamWriter("sample.txt"); writer.WriteLine("This program is writing"); writer.WriteLine("our first file."); writer.Close(); } } } Look at the code: - The `System.IO` namespace: : - Namespace: Note the `using System.IO` namespace being used at the top. It gives the program access to the functionalities in the System.IO namespace. For your current concern, this means a number of classes that contains many **methods** that you use. - You will always need to be using `System.IO` when working with files. Here is a slightly different use of a dot, `.`, to indicate a *subsidiary* namespace. Under System.IO, there are plenty of classes (with methods defined inside) for system IO operations, such as: \- File, \- StreamWriter, \- FileStream, \- StreamReader, \- Directory, \- Path, etc. - The StreamWriter Class: : - variable: The first line of the body of `Main` creates a `StreamWriter` object assigned to the variable `writer`. - A `StreamWriter` links C# to your computer's file system for writing, not reading. - Files are objects, like a Random, and you use the `new` syntax to create a new one. - The StreamWriter class parameter ("constructor", to be covered in later chapters) gives the name of the file to connect to the program, `sample.txt`, which is the same as the file name we saw created by the program. :::{warning} If the file already existed, the old contents are *destroyed* silently by creating a `StreamWriter`. ::: - writer.WriteLine(): The writer variable is of data type (or just type) StreamWriter and StreamWriter has method WriteLine() just like the Console class. The difference is that Console.WriteLine writes to the console/terminal, whereas StreamWriter.WriteLine writes out a data stream to a file followed by a newline character. ```{index} StreamWriter; format string StreamWriter; Write ``` :::{note} Just as you can use a {ref}`Format-Strings` with functions `Write` and `WriteLine` of the `Console` class, you can also use a format string with the corresponding methods of a `StreamWriter`, and embed fields by using braces in the format string. ::: - writer.Close(): The Close() method closes the current StreamWriter object and the underlying stream. The Close() method is important for cleaning up. Until this line, this C# program controls the file, and nothing may be actually written to the operating system file yet: Since initiating a file operation is thousands of times slower than memory operations, C# *buffers* data, saving small amounts and writing a larger chunk all at once. :::{warning} The call to the `Close` method is essential for C# to make sure everything is really written, and to relinquish control of the file for use by other programs. It is a common bug to write a program where you have the code to add all the data you want to a file, but the program does not end up creating a file. Usually this means you forgot to close the file! ::: ```{index} StreamReader; read and close ``` ```{index} StreamReader ``` (fileread)= ## `StreamReader` In the sample code (`first_file.cs`) of Writing Files from last section, you specified a file {file}`sample.txt`, which currently exists in the present project folder. The code is as seen below: using System; using System.IO; namespace IntroCSCS { class Ch07File // basics of file writing { public static void Main() { StreamWriter writer = new StreamWriter("sample.txt"); writer.WriteLine("This program is writing"); writer.WriteLine("our first file."); writer.Close(); } } } Now, take a look at the following code (`print_first_file.cs`) and compare to the code above (`first_file.cs`): using System; using System.IO; namespace IntroCSCS { class PrintFirstFile // basics of reading file lines { public static void Main() { // Setup: create sample.txt (same as first_file.cs) so this cell runs on its own. StreamWriter writer = new StreamWriter("sample.txt"); writer.WriteLine("This program is writing"); writer.WriteLine("our first file."); writer.Close(); StreamReader reader = new StreamReader("sample.txt"); string line = reader.ReadLine(); // first line // string? ==> nullable Console.WriteLine(line); line = reader.ReadLine(); // second line Console.WriteLine(line); reader.Close(); } } } Now you have read a file and used it in a program. In the first line of `Main`, the file (`sample.txt`) is again associated with a C# variable name (`reader`), this time for reading as a `StreamReader`, instead of a `StreamWriter`, object. A `StreamReader` can only open an existing file, so `sample.txt` must already exist. Again we have parallel names to those used with `Console`, but in this case the `ReadLine` method returns the next line from the file. Here the string from the file line is assigned to the variable `line`. Each call the ReadLine reads the next line of the file. Such behavior is similar to the `Console.ReadLine()` that you know about but different as `StreamReader.ReadLine()` reads the next line from the input `stream` (or null if the end of the input stream is reached) rather than from user command line input. Finally, using the `Close` method is generally optional with files being read. There is nothing to lose if a program ends without closing a file that was being read. ```{index} StreamReader; EndOfStream EndOfStream ``` ```{index} Reading to End of Stream ``` ```{index} Reading to End of Stream ``` (endofstream)= ## Reading to End of Stream In `first_file.cs`, we explicitly coded reading two lines. You will often want to process each line in a file, without knowing the total number of lines at the time when you were programming. This means that files provide us with our second kind of a `sequence`: the sequence of lines in the file! To process all of them will require a loop and a new test to make sure that you have not yet come to the end of the file's stream: You can use the `EndOfStream` property. It has the wrong sense (true at the end of the file), so we negate it, testing for `!reader.EndOfStream` to *continue* reading. The example program `print_file_lines.cs` below reads and prints the contents of a file specified by the user, one line at a time: using System; using System.IO; namespace IntroCSCS { class PrintFileLines // demo of using EndOfStream test { public static void Main() { // Setup: create sample.txt (same as first_file.cs) so this cell runs on its own. StreamWriter writer = new StreamWriter("sample.txt"); writer.WriteLine("This program is writing"); writer.WriteLine("our first file."); writer.Close(); Console.Write("Enter name of file to print: "); string userFileName = Console.ReadLine(); if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(userFileName)) { userFileName = "sample.txt"; // no input given: use the setup file } var reader = new StreamReader(userFileName); while (!reader.EndOfStream) { string line = reader.ReadLine(); Console.WriteLine(line); } reader.Close(); } } } ```{index} var type; var ``` `var` > For conciseness (and variety) we declared `reader` > using the more compact syntax with `var`: > > ``` > var reader = new StreamReader(userFileName); > ``` > > You can use `var` in place of a declared type to shorten your code > with a couple of restrictions: > > - Use an initializer, from which the type of the variable can be inferred. > - Declare a local variable inside a method body or in a loop heading. > - Declare only a single variable in the statement. > > We could have used this syntax long ago, but as the type names become longer, > it is more useful! You can run this program. You need an existing file to read. An obvious file is the source file itself: {file}`print_file_lines.cs`. Or, if you have implemented/tested the files by placing the code in your `Program.cs`, you may use the `sample.txt` file here. In the latter case, you should see: ``` Enter name of file to print: sample.txt This program is writing our first file. ``` Things to note about reading from files: ```{index} StreamReader; null from ReadLine ``` - Reading from a file returns the part read, of course. Never forget the *side effect*: The location in the file advances past the part just read. The next read does *not* return the *same* thing as last time. It returns the *next* part of the file. - Our `while` test conditions so far have been in a sense "backward looking": We have tested a variable that has *already been set*. The test with `EndOfStream` is *forward looking*: looking at what has not been processed yet. Other than making sure the file is opened, there is no variable that needs to be set before a `while` loop testing for `EndOfStream`. - If you use ReadLine at the end of the file, the special value `null` (no object) is returned. *This* is not an error, but if you try to apply any string methods to the `null` value returned, *then* you get an error! Though `print_file_lines.cs` was a nice simple illustration of a loop reading lines, it was very verbose considering the final effect of the program, just to print the whole file. You can read the entire remaining contents of a file as a single (multiline) string, using the `StreamReader` method `ReadToEnd`. In place of the reading and printing loop we could have just had: using System; using System.IO; namespace IntroCSCS { class PrintWholeFile // demo of ReadToEnd { public static void Main() { // Setup: create sample.txt (same as first_file.cs) so this cell runs on its own. StreamWriter writer = new StreamWriter("sample.txt"); writer.WriteLine("This program is writing"); writer.WriteLine("our first file."); writer.Close(); var reader = new StreamReader("sample.txt"); string wholeFile = reader.ReadToEnd(); // replaces the while loop Console.Write(wholeFile); reader.Close(); } } } `ReadToEnd` does not strip off a newline, unlike `ReadLine`, so we do not want to add an extra newline when writing. Here we can use the `Write` method instead of `WriteLine`. % .. [#readclose] % If, for some reason, you want to reread this same file while the % same program is running, you need to close it and reopen it. % .. [#finalNewline] % Besides the speed and efficiency of this second approach, % there is also a technical improvement: There may or may not be % a newline at the end of the very last line of the file. The ``ReadLine`` % method works either way, but does not let you know the difference. % In the line-by-line version, there is always a newline after the % final line written with ``WriteLine``. % The ``ReadToEnd`` version will have newlines exactly matching the input. ```{index} Directory path ``` ```{index} Directory path ``` ### Directory path If you do not use any operating system directory separators in the name (`'\'` or `'/'`, depending on your operating system), then the file will lie in the **current directory**. For example, you may create a `data` directory under your introcscs directory and place all data files in it. ```{rubric} Footnotes ``` [^0902_file_operations-constructor]: The concept and use of constructor will be covered in subsequent chapters regarding object-oriented programming.

# File Workflows, Paths, and Resources


```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```


```{index} Separate a File's Location from Its Contents
```



```{index} Run a Complete File Lifetime in an Owned Workspace
```

## Run a Complete File Lifetime in an Owned Workspace


A report has two different identities: its contents and its location. Reading valid quantities from the wrong file is still a failed workflow. Start by constructing one known path, use it consistently, and make ownership of temporary files explicit. This connects Chapter 6's cleanup policy with the stream operations introduced in the preceding section.

`Path.Combine(directory, fileName)` returns a string using the platform's path rules. It does not create a directory or a file. `Directory.CreateDirectory(path)` creates the directory if needed. The general using-statement form is a syntax pattern:

```text
using (ResourceType name = acquireResource())
{
    statementsThatUse(name);
}
```

The closing brace marks disposal of the acquired resource. The related declaration form, `using ResourceType name = acquireResource();`, keeps the resource until the end of its enclosing scope. Choose the scope deliberately: a writer must be disposed before another operation relies on its completed output.

This example creates a uniquely named temporary directory owned by this run, writes two lines, closes the writer, reads those lines, closes the reader, and deletes only that owned directory. It does not overwrite a student's report or depend on a preexisting file.


using System;
using System.IO;
string workspace = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "cscs_report_" + Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N"));
Directory.CreateDirectory(workspace);
try
{
    string reportPath = Path.Combine(workspace, "report.txt");
    using (StreamWriter writer = new StreamWriter(reportPath, append: false))
    {
        writer.WriteLine("Order 101");
        writer.WriteLine("Units 3");
    }
    using (StreamReader reader = new StreamReader(reportPath))
    {
        Console.WriteLine(reader.ReadLine());
        Console.WriteLine(reader.ReadLine());
        Console.WriteLine($"At end: {reader.EndOfStream}");
    }
    Console.WriteLine($"Exists before cleanup: {File.Exists(reportPath)}");
}
finally
{
    Directory.Delete(workspace, recursive: true);
}
Console.WriteLine($"Directory remains: {Directory.Exists(workspace)}");


Each using block releases its stream when the block ends, even if processing leaves it because of an exception. The outer finally attempts workspace cleanup after the streams have been disposed. Cleanup can itself fail in a real application; finally does not grant permissions or guarantee that a disk operation will succeed.

| Point in this program | Resource state | What is established |
| --- | --- | --- |
| After constructing reportPath | No report opened yet | A location string exists |
| Inside writer block | Writer open | Lines are being written |
| After writer block | Writer disposed | Buffered output has been finalized normally |
| Inside reader block | Reader open | The same path is being consumed |
| After reader block | Reader disposed | No stream from this example remains open |
| After finally succeeds | Owned directory removed | The example's temporary files are gone |

`Exists` being true does not prove that the report contains valid business data. Conversely, an exception while opening a missing input does not mean that a report contains zero records. Keep “no readable input” separate from “readable input containing no rows.”


```{index} Predict Append and Missing-Input Outcomes
```

## Predict Append and Missing-Input Outcomes


Guided exercise: before the reader block, open a second writer with `append: true` and write `Status ready`. Change the reader to a loop that reads until ReadLine returns null. Predict three printed lines and explain why overwrite mode would instead destroy the first two lines. Derive the expected result before changing the code.

For a deterministic missing-input case, the next example uses a fresh owned directory and deliberately never creates the requested file. It catches FileNotFoundException, rather than presenting the operation as a successful empty import.


using System;
using System.IO;
string workspace = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "cscs_missing_" + Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N"));
Directory.CreateDirectory(workspace);
try
{
    string inputPath = Path.Combine(workspace, "not_created.txt");
    try
    {
        using StreamReader reader = new StreamReader(inputPath);
        Console.WriteLine(reader.ReadToEnd());
    }
    catch (FileNotFoundException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Input unavailable; import did not run.");
    }
}
finally { Directory.Delete(workspace, recursive: true); }


A production caller may also need policies for access denial and other I/O failures, as in the retained examples. An existence check before opening is not a replacement for handling the open itself: another process could change the file between the check and the operation. For independent transfer in the chapter assignments, state the file location, write mode, invalid-record policy and cleanup owner before writing the import.


```{index} Separate a File's Location from Its Contents
```

## Separate a File's Location from Its Contents



A report can contain perfectly valid text and still fail to open because its path names the wrong location. A relative path is interpreted from the process's working directory, which need not be the directory containing the source file. Before changing your parsing code, establish which file the program is actually trying to open.

The resource workflow is a sequence: choose the location, acquire the resource, process data, and release the resource. Reading and writing are separate contracts. Overwriting a report, appending a new entry, and reading an existing log are not interchangeable operations just because they share a path.

| Question | Example consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Is the path relative or absolute? | Running from another working directory can select another file |
| Must the file already exist? | A missing input is different from a new output |
| May existing contents be replaced? | Opening the wrong write mode can destroy a previous report |
| Who owns the open resource? | Cleanup must occur even if processing stops early |

Use Path.Combine to assemble path components for the current platform rather than hard-coding one separator convention. This constructs a path string; it does not create directories, grant permissions, or prove that an input file exists. Likewise, checking existence before opening cannot guarantee that a later open succeeds: resource state can change between those operations.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


```{index} Bound Resource Lifetime Explicitly
```



```{index} Bound Resource Lifetime Explicitly
```

## Bound Resource Lifetime Explicitly



A StreamReader or StreamWriter owns resources that must be disposed. A using statement or declaration expresses that lifetime. The general declaration form is `using ResourceType name = acquisitionExpression;`; this is a syntax pattern. Processing statements use that acquired resource inside its permitted scope. Disposal handles resource release; it does not establish that every record was valid or that a business transaction completed successfully.

For an input import, distinguish two outcomes: the resource cannot be opened, or a particular line has invalid data. The first may prevent the whole import. The second may permit recording the line number and continuing, if that is the stated policy. Do not catch an unavailable-file exception and silently report that zero valid records were found; zero records and no readable input are different outcomes.

Guided scenario: a program writes the first two report lines and then fails on the third. What does cleanup guarantee, and what does it not guarantee? It releases owned resources during normal exception unwinding, but it does not magically restore the previous complete report. Reliable replacement may require writing a separate temporary file and a deliberate publication step. That design is an extension; recognizing partial output is already part of understanding the current contract.

(path-strings)=

## Path Strings




When a program is running, there is alway a *current directory* (or,
**present working directory**, `pwd`). Files in the present working directory can
be referred to by their simple names, e.g., *sample.txt*, so
project files can be referred to by their simple names because they are in the same
directory.

Referring to files not in the current directory is more complicated.
You should be aware from using the Windows Explorer or the macOS Finder that
files and directories are located in a hierarchy of directories in the
file system. On a Mac, the file system is unified in
one hierarchy. On Windows, each storage drive has its own hierarchy.

```{index} path separator
```

Files are generally referred to by a chain of directories before
the final name of the file desired. A *path string* (or simply **path**) is used
to represent such a sequence of names. Elements of the directory chain are separated
by operating system specific punctuation symbols: In Windows the separator is
backslash, `\`, and on a Mac it is (forward) slash, `/`. For example, on a Mac the path

```none
/Users/anh
```

starts with a /, meaning the **root** or top directory in the hierarchy, and Users is
a subdirectory, and anh is a subdirectory of Users (in this case the home directory
for the user with login anh). It is similar with Windows, except there may be a drive
in the beginning, and the separator is a \\, so

```none
C:\Windows\System32
```

is on C: drive; Windows is a subdirectory of the root directory \\, and System32 is
a subdirectory of Windows. Each drive in Windows has a separate file hierarchy
underneath it.

```{index} path; absolute
```

Paths starting from the root of a file system, with `\` or `/` are called
**absolute paths** or **full paths** because they begin with the root of the file hierarchy.
Since there is always a current directory, it makes sense to allow a path to be *relative*
to the current directory. In that case do *not* start with the slash that would
indicate the root directory. For example, if the current directory is
your user home directory, you likely have a subdirectory {file}`Downloads`, and the
{file}`Downloads` directory might contain {file}`examples.zip`. From the home directory,
this file could be referred to as {file}`Downloads\\examples.zip` in Windows or
{file}`Downloads/examples.zip` on a Mac.

Referring to files in the current directory just by their plain file name is
actually an example of using relative paths.

```{index} parent folder (..)
```

With relative paths, you sometimes want to move up the directory hierarchy: `..`
(two periods) refers to the directory one level up the chain.

For example, suppose you have a `data` directory under your `introcscs` directory,
and you place your sample.txt in the data directory. When running your project from the
project directory (Ch07File), you would refer to the sample.txt file to read as
{file}`..\\data\\sample.txt` in Windows or
{file}`../data/sample.txt` in macOS. Follow this one step at a time:
Starting from the {file}`Ch07File` project folder, where the program is running,
go up one folder ({file}`..`) to the `introcscs` folder, then down into the
{file}`data` folder, and refer to the {file}`sample.txt` file in that folder.

```{index} current folder (.)
```

Occasionally you need to
refer explicitly to the current directory: It is referred to as {file}`.`. (a single
period).

```{index} Path class
```



```{index} Paths in C#
```



```{index} Paths in C\#
```

## Paths in C\#




The differing versions of paths for Windows and a Mac are a pain to deal with. Luckily C#
abstracts away the differences. It has a `Path` class in the `System.IO`
namespace that provides many handy functions for dealing with paths in
an operating system independent way:

For one thing, C# knows the path separator character for your operating system,
`Path.DirectorySeparatorChar`.

More useful is the function `Path.Combine`, which takes any number of string parameters
for sequential parts of a path, and creates a single string appropriate for the
current operating system. For example,
`Path.Combine("bin", "Debug")` will return `"bin\Debug"` or `"bin/debug"`
as appropriate.
`Path.Combine("..", "data", "sample.txt")` will return a string with characters
`..\data\sample.txt` or `../data/sample.txt`.

Even if you know you are going to be on Windows, file paths are a problem because
`\` is the string escape character. To enter the Windows path solve explicitly
you would need to have `"..\\data\\sample.txt"`, or the raw string prefix,
`@` can come to the rescue: `@"..\data\sample.txt"`.

Path strings are used by the {ref}`directory-class` and by the {ref}`file-class`.
You can look at the `Path` class in the C# Language Reference
for many other operations with path strings.


```{index} The Directory Class
```



```{index} The Directory Class
```

(directory-class)=

## The Directory Class




The `Directory` class is in the `System.IO` namespace.
Directories in the file system are referenced by {ref}`path-strings`.
You can look at the C# language reference for a wide variety of functions in the
`Directory` class including ones to list all the files in a directory
or to check if a path string represents an actual directory.


This chapter shows how to define classes, create instances, protect data, and build reusable types. - **Class**: A class defines the fields, properties, constructors, and methods for a kind of object. - **Instance**: An instance is a concrete object created from a class. - **Encapsulation**: Encapsulation keeps data inside an object and exposes controlled operations. - **Constructor**: A constructor initializes a new object into a valid starting state. - **Property**: A property provides controlled access to object state. title: Object Design and Composition
source:
# Object Design and Composition A useful application needs more than individually correct classes. This chapter connects objects into a small business model and makes their ownership, sharing, and failure policies explicit. - **Reference**: A value identifying an object; several variables may refer to one object. - **Identity**: Whether references identify the same runtime object. - **Composition**: Building an object from smaller objects with defined responsibilities. - **Immutability**: Keeping observable state fixed after construction. - **Contract**: The promised results and failure behavior of public operations.

Learning Objectives

1. Trace aliases and distinguish object identity from business equality. 2. Explain the effect of sharing mutable and immutable objects, and distinguish struct copying from record-class copying and equality. 3. Design collaborating product, order-line, and order classes. 4. Protect a private collection and explain shallow snapshot behavior. 5. Test boundaries and refactor while preserving observable behavior. 6. Distinguish required and optional object data, interpret nullable warnings, and test missing-data contracts.

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`11.1. References, Identity, and Copying <1101_objects_references>` - {doc}`11.2. Structs, Records, and Data Models <1105_value_record_types>` - {doc}`11.3. Composition and Object Responsibilities <1102_composition>` - {doc}`11.4. Testing and Refactoring Collaborating Objects <1103_testing_collaboration>` - {doc}`11.5. Nullability and Missing Data (Supporting reading) <1104_nullability>`

Glossary

| Term | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Struct | A user-defined value type whose value is copied on assignment. | | Record | A class or struct with compiler-generated data-oriented members, including value-based equality. | | Alias | Another reference to the same object. | | Identity | Being the same runtime object. | | Business equality | Matching according to an explicit domain rule. | | Mutable | Allowing observable state to change after construction. | | Immutable | Keeping observable state fixed after construction. | | Composition | A has-a relationship among collaborating objects. | | Responsibility | A coherent job assigned to a type. | | Shallow copy | A copy of immediate values and references. | | Invariant | A rule preserved at public operation boundaries. | | Refactoring | Changing internal design while preserving intended behavior. |

Lecture Slides

Slides and a chapter video remain pending. The three content notebooks form the teaching sequence.

2. Explain the effect of sharing mutable and immutable objects, and distinguish struct copying from record-class copying and equality.
3. Design collaborating product, order-line, and order classes.
4. Protect a private collection and explain shallow snapshot behavior.
5. Test boundaries and refactor while preserving observable behavior.
6. Distinguish required and optional object data, interpret nullable warnings, and test missing-data contracts.

sections.Glossary:
| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Struct | A user-defined value type whose value is copied on assignment. |
| Record | A class or struct with compiler-generated data-oriented members, including value-based equality. |
| Alias | Another reference to the same object. |
| Identity | Being the same runtime object. |
| Business equality | Matching according to an explicit domain rule. |
| Mutable | Allowing observable state to change after construction. |
| Immutable | Keeping observable state fixed after construction. |
| Composition | A has-a relationship among collaborating objects. |
| Responsibility | A coherent job assigned to a type. |
| Shallow copy | A copy of immediate values and references. |
| Invariant | A rule preserved at public operation boundaries. |
| Refactoring | Changing internal design while preserving intended behavior. |

title: Inheritance, Interfaces, and Polymorphism
source:
# Inheritance, Interfaces, and Polymorphism This chapter builds on ordinary composition to support clients that work with different implementations of one behavior. - **Inheritance**: A derived type builds on a base type while preserving its behavioral promises. - **Polymorphism**: A common client call uses the implementation associated with an actual object. - **Abstract class**: A general type that requires concrete derived behavior and can supply shared state or methods. - **Interface**: A named capability contract implemented by different classes. - **Substitution**: Using one implementation without breaking the expectations of clients of the general type.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: PmKlPGp0O5w :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[C# for Beginners – Lesson 15: Inheritance, Polymorphism & Abstraction](https://youtube.com/watch?v=PmKlPGp0O5w)* by Mike's Code. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

1. Construct a small hierarchy with validated base and derived state. 2. Explain virtual dispatch and distinguish overriding from overloading. 3. Implement concrete behavior for an abstract class. 4. Supply interchangeable components through interfaces and constructors. 5. Test shared contracts and choose composition or inheritance from requirements.

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`12.1. Inheritance and Substitution <1201_inheritance>` - {doc}`12.2. Runtime Polymorphism and Abstract Classes <1202_polymorphism>` - {doc}`12.3. Interfaces and Interchangeable Components <1203_interfaces>` - {doc}`12.4. OOP Examples and Variations (Supporting reading) <1204_oop_examples>`

Glossary

| Term | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Base class | A type inherited by a derived class. | | Derived class | A type extending one base class. | | Override | A replacement implementation for an inherited virtual or abstract member. | | Runtime dispatch | Selecting an override according to the actual object. | | Overload | A same-name method with a different parameter list. | | Abstract class | A class that cannot be instantiated directly. | | Interface | A named capability contract. | | Substitution | Using an implementation through a general type while preserving client expectations. | | Constructor injection | Supplying a collaborator when constructing its client. | | Test double | A controlled replacement used to observe or check collaboration. |

Lecture Slides

Slides remain pending while the revised content stabilizes.

Optional Business Application Extensions

After the core OOP sequence, apply these ideas through the {doc}`database capstone <../appendices/databases/index>` or the {doc}`AI application project extension <../appendices/project/ai_extension>`. Databases add persistent records; the AI extension adds a reviewed suggestion through an interchangeable component. Either track is optional; CS1 is complete without them.
