# ADT Contracts

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

An **abstract data type** starts with behavior. Before deciding whether data should be stored in an array, linked nodes, or a hash table, we decide what operations the type promises to support.


```{index} Describe the Observable History First
```



```{index} Describe the Observable History First
```

## Describe the Observable History First



An undo history is not defined by an array or a linked node. It is defined by what a client can observe after a sequence of operations. If the client records A, records B, and then undoes once, it expects B to be removed before A. An implementation can store those entries in different ways while preserving that behavior. This separates the abstract data type, the behavioral contract, from the data structure used to realize it.

Write the history on paper before writing a class. For each operation, record the result, the resulting abstract contents, and the empty/failure policy. If the contract says an unsuccessful TryPop leaves state unchanged, returning false after already decrementing Count violates the contract even if later tests happen to restore the count.

| Operation | Result | Abstract history, oldest to newest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start | Empty | [] |
| Push A | Recorded | [A] |
| Push B | Recorded | [A, B] |
| TryPop | Success, B | [A] |
| TryPop | Success, A | [] |
| TryPop | Failure | [] |

The empty failure is part of the behavior, not an implementation detail to settle later. A different ADT might throw on an empty Pop. Both can be coherent contracts, but a client written for one cannot assume the other. Also specify whether null entries, duplicates, or a fixed capacity are allowed. These policies determine which tests should succeed and what failure must preserve.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


```{index} Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge
```



```{index} Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge
```

## Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge



A C# interface can express operation names and types, for example a success-returning method with an out result. It cannot by itself express every ordering rule or state invariant. Two classes can compile against the same interface and still behave differently. Tests and explanations connect the syntax to the promised history.

The client should not need to know the backing array's capacity or the head node's field name. If a capacity change affects returned values or exposes unused slots, representation details have leaked through the abstraction. Conversely, the implementer must know enough about storage to maintain its invariants. Abstraction assigns different responsibilities to the two roles; it does not mean that implementation details are unimportant.

Guided exercise: keep the interface unchanged but change removal to return A before B. Identify the first row at which this behavior differs from the specified history. Then explain why a test that checks only Count would miss the defect. Extend the history with a failed removal followed by a new push; this checks whether failure left the structure reusable.

```{dropdown} Contract checkpoint
The first successful removal must return B. A queue-like implementation could keep the right counts while returning the wrong element. Checking returned values, order, state after failure, and later reuse tests more of the contract than checking size alone.
```


```{index} abstract data type
```
```{index} contract; data structure
```



```{index} What an ADT Specifies
```

## What an ADT Specifies



An ADT describes a set of values and the operations allowed on those values. It does **not** require one particular internal representation.

For a stack, the contract might say:

| Operation | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Push(item)` | Add an item to the top. |
| `Pop()` | Remove and return the top item. |
| `Peek()` | Return the top item without removing it. |
| `Count` | Report how many items are stored. |

This contract says nothing about arrays or linked lists. That separation is the point: client code should depend on the behavior it needs, not on accidental implementation details.


```{index} interface; ADT
```



```{index} Interfaces as Contracts
```

## Interfaces as Contracts



In C#, an `interface` is a natural way to write an ADT contract. It names the operations but leaves the storage strategy to a class.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
IStack<string> history = new ListStack<string>();
history.Push("open file");
history.Push("rename variable");
Console.WriteLine(history.Pop());
Console.WriteLine(history.Peek());

interface IStack<T>
{
    int Count { get; }
    void Push(T item);
    T Pop();
    T Peek();
}

class ListStack<T> : IStack<T>
{
    private readonly List<T> items = new();
    public int Count => items.Count;

    public void Push(T item) => items.Add(item);

    public T Pop()
    {
        if (items.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Stack is empty.");
        int last = items.Count - 1;
        T value = items[last];
        items.RemoveAt(last);
        return value;
    }

    public T Peek()
    {
        if (items.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Stack is empty.");
        return items[^1];
    }
}

```{index} client code
```



```{index} Client Code Depends on Behavior
```

## Client Code Depends on Behavior



**Client code** is code that uses a type. If client code only needs stack behavior, it should not care whether the stack is backed by a `List<T>`, an array, or linked nodes.

That means this is a better variable type for many methods:

```csharp
static void UndoLastAction(IStack<string> actions)
```

than this:

```csharp
static void UndoLastAction(ListStack<string> actions)
```

The first version accepts any stack implementation that satisfies the contract.


```{index} invariant
```



```{index} Contracts Include Rules
```

## Contracts Include Rules



A contract includes more than method names. It also includes rules:

- `Pop` removes the same item that `Peek` would return.
- `Count` increases after `Push` and decreases after `Pop`.
- `Pop` and `Peek` on an empty stack are errors.

A rule that must remain true for the object to be valid is called an **invariant**. Data-structure code often exists to preserve invariants while operations run quickly.


```{index} Practice
```

## Practice



1. Write a contract for a queue ADT using operation names and meanings.
2. Name one invariant a queue implementation must preserve.
3. Explain why a method parameter typed as `IStack<string>` is more flexible than one typed as `ListStack<string>`.


```{index} Summary
```

## Summary



An ADT names behavior. An interface can express that behavior in C#. Implementations provide storage and algorithms behind the contract. This separation lets programs change representation without changing every caller.


```{rubric} Footnotes
```


[^1301_adt_contracts-1]: Some C# library types use classes directly instead of exposing a small custom interface. The ADT idea still helps you reason about what behavior the code depends on.


[^development-reading]: Further reading: [OpenDSA, Lists: Chapter Introduction](https://opendsa.org/OpenDSA/Books/Catalog/html/ListIntro.html). The worked business scenarios and guided reasoning here are original teaching examples.

# Linear Lists This chapter covers array-backed lists, dynamic arrays, linked nodes, linked lists, and the operation-cost tradeoffs between contiguous and linked sequence representations. The sidebar title **Linear Lists** names the shared idea: data arranged in a single sequence. - **Contiguous storage**: Array-backed sequences keep elements next to each other for fast indexed access. - **Dynamic array**: A dynamic array grows by allocating larger storage and copying existing values. - **Linked node**: A linked structure stores values in nodes connected by references. - **Insertion and deletion**: Different representations make middle updates cheaper or more expensive. - **Performance tradeoff**: Choosing a sequence representation depends on access, growth, and update patterns. Arrays and linked lists make the connection between memory representation and program behavior visible.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: RBSGKlAvoiM :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[Data Structures Easy to Advanced Course - Full Tutorial from a Google Engineer](https://youtube.com/watch?v=RBSGKlAvoiM)* by freeCodeCamp.org. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Explain how array-based and linked representations store sequence data 2. Trace resizing, shifting, and the total copy cost of repeated appends 3. Implement generic array-backed and singly linked sequences, preserving count, head, and tail invariants 4. Compare indexed access, search, insertion, and deletion costs 5. Test empty, singleton, duplicate, and invalid-index cases and justify a representation for a specific workload 6. Select linear or binary search and prepare a sorted report with explicit mutation and tie policies.

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`14.1. Dynamic Arrays <1401_dynamic_arrays>` - {doc}`14.2. Linked Nodes <1402_linked_nodes>` - {doc}`14.3. Representation Tradeoffs and Verification <1403_comparison_lab>`

Glossary

| # | Term | Explanation | |---:|---|---| | 1 | Linear list | A sequence of items arranged in order. | | 2 | Array representation | A sequence representation that stores items in contiguous indexed positions. | | 3 | Linked representation | A sequence representation where nodes refer to neighboring nodes. | | 4 | Dynamic array | An array-backed list that resizes when it needs more capacity. | | 5 | Capacity | The number of items an underlying array can currently hold. | | 6 | Resize | Allocating a larger array and copying items into it. | | 7 | Node | An object that stores one value and one or more links. | | 8 | Link | A reference from one node to another. | | 9 | Head | The first node in a linked list. | | 10 | Tail | The last node in a linked list. | | 11 | Traversal | Visiting list items from one position to the next. | | 12 | Insertion | Adding a new item to a sequence. | | 13 | Deletion | Removing an item from a sequence. | | 14 | Indexed access | Retrieving an item by numeric position. | | 15 | Search cost | The work needed to find a value in a sequence. | | 16 | Amortized cost | Total work over a sequence of operations divided by its length. | | 17 | Invariant | A representation rule preserved by every completed operation. | | 18 | Memory locality | Accessing storage locations close together, often helping sequential access. | | 19 | Linear search | Scan records until a matching item is found or input ends. | | 20 | Binary search | Repeatedly narrow a sorted random-access interval. | | 21 | Stable sorting | Preserve arrival order among items with equal comparison keys. |

# Representation Tradeoffs and Verification

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

This lab compares array-backed and linked-node representations by counting visits and explaining tradeoffs. The goal is not to prove that one representation is always better. The goal is to connect a workload to a representation choice.


```{index} Array Search and Indexing
```



```{index} Array Search and Indexing
```

## Array Search and Indexing



Arrays are strong at indexing. Searching by value still requires checking elements until the value is found or the array ends.


int[] values = { 12, 7, 19, 4, 15 };

int visits = 0;
int target = 15;
for (int index = 0; index < values.Length; index++)
{
    visits++;
    if (values[index] == target)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Found {target} at index {index} after {visits} visits.");
        break;
    }
}

Console.WriteLine($"Direct index values[2] = {values[2]}");


```{index} Linked Traversal
```



```{index} Linked Traversal
```

## Linked Traversal



A linked representation visits nodes by following references. There is no direct index jump.


Node<int> head = new Node<int>(12);
head.Next = new Node<int>(7);
head.Next.Next = new Node<int>(19);
head.Next.Next.Next = new Node<int>(4);
head.Next.Next.Next.Next = new Node<int>(15);

int visits = 0;
int target = 15;
for (Node<int>? current = head; current is not null; current = current.Next)
{
    visits++;
    if (current.Value == target)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Found {target} after {visits} node visits.");
        break;
    }
}

public class Node<T>
{
    public T Value { get; }
    public Node<T>? Next { get; set; }
    public Node(T value) => Value = value;
}

```{index} Middle Insertion Costs
```



```{index} Middle Insertion Costs
```

## Middle Insertion Costs



In an array, inserting into the middle requires shifting later elements. In a linked list, insertion after a known node changes references locally, but finding that node may still require traversal.


int[] values = new int[6] { 10, 20, 40, 50, 0, 0 };
int count = 4;
int insertIndex = 2;
int shifts = 0;

for (int i = count; i > insertIndex; i--)
{
    values[i] = values[i - 1];
    shifts++;
}

values[insertIndex] = 30;
count++;

Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", values[..count]));
Console.WriteLine($"shifts={shifts}");


```{index} Decision Guide
```



```{index} Decision Guide
```

## Decision Guide



| Workload | Better starting representation | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frequent indexing | Dynamic array | O(1) direct access by index |
| Frequent append | Dynamic array | Amortized O(1) append |
| Frequent insertion after known nodes | Linked list | O(1) reference update |
| Frequent search by value | Neither is ideal alone | Both may scan O(n) |
| Low per-item memory overhead | Dynamic array | No per-node reference field |

Use this table as a starting point, then adjust based on real operation counts and program constraints.


```{index} Lab Tasks
```



```{index} Lab Tasks
```

## Lab Tasks



1. Change the target in both search examples to the first, middle, last, and missing values. Record visit counts.
2. Modify the array insertion example to insert at the front. How many shifts are required?
3. Write a linked-list `CountNodes` method and test it with empty, one-node, and three-node lists.
4. Choose a representation for a playlist app where users often skip by index.
5. Choose a representation for a simulation where events are frequently inserted after a known event node.


```{index} workload; operation count; representation comparison
```



```{index} Separate Location Cost from Update Cost
```

## Separate Location Cost from Update Cost



A service desk stores `n` work orders. Two requests that sound similar can require different work: “insert at position 400” supplies an index; “insert after this node” supplies a location handle. Compare the same request and the same assumptions before claiming a speed advantage.

| Request | Dynamic array | Singly linked list with head and tail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read index i | O(1) | O(i + 1), O(n) worst case |
| Append | O(1) amortized, O(n) on resize | O(1) with stored tail |
| Insert at front | O(n) shifts | O(1) |
| Insert by index in middle | O(n) shifts, possibly growth | O(n) locate, O(1) rewire |
| Remove by index in middle | O(n) shifts | O(n) locate, O(1) rewire |
| Remove last | O(1), without shrinking | O(n) find predecessor |
| Search unsorted values | O(n) | O(n) |
| Visit every item once | O(n) | O(n) with cursor |

The linked wrapper in this chapter exposes indices rather than public node handles. Its middle insertion therefore includes traversal. A different API could expose validated handles, but it must specify ownership and what happens when a handle refers to a removed node.

**Reason (applied):** A developer claims `Insert(400, value)` is constant-time because it changes two links. Identify the omitted work. Would adding a tail field fix it?

```{index} operation count; workload model
```



```{index} Count a Concrete Workload
```

## Count a Concrete Workload



Use eight initial orders and spare array capacity. Compare a front insertion, a last-position read, and a front removal.

| Operation | Array work | Linked work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insert at front | Eight existing-value shifts | No link traversal; update head |
| Read last position after insertion | One indexed read | Eight link advances from head |
| Remove front | Eight existing-value shifts | No link traversal; update head |

If readers request the last position 100 times between these updates, the array uses 100 indexed reads while the linked sequence uses 800 link advances. If the workload instead performs many front updates and few index reads, the preference may reverse. Include the whole operation mix.

Counts of different primitives are not interchangeable seconds. Copying a reference, following a link, allocating a node, and checking a bound have different costs. Counts explain how work grows; benchmarks answer a narrower question about a specific implementation and machine.

**Transfer (challenge):** Compare 100 last-index reads plus one front insertion for 1,000 orders. State your assumptions about spare capacity and any stored tail. Then change the request to “read the tail value.” Explain why changing the API changes the comparison.

```{index} boundary tests; invariants; sequence contract
```



```{index} Test the Contract Before Comparing Speed
```

## Test the Contract Before Comparing Speed



Both implementations should produce the same logical result for the same legal operation sequence. Test correctness first. A fast implementation that loses an order is not an alternative representation of the same ADT.

| Test | Operations | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty start | Construct | Count zero; read index zero throws. |
| Single element | Add A; remove index zero | Returns A; count zero. |
| Reuse after emptying | Previous test; add B | Read index zero returns B. |
| Middle insertion | Add A, C; insert B at one | A, B, C in that order. |
| Middle removal | Previous test; remove one | Returns B; leaves A, C. |
| Duplicate values | Add A twice; remove zero | One A remains. |
| Invalid insertion | Insert at count plus one | Throws; count and contents unchanged. |
| Invalid removal | Remove at count | Throws; count and contents unchanged. |

Do not test only printed output from the happy path. Check count after each operation, and verify remaining values after removal. A useful additional check compares a generated operation sequence against C# `List<T>` as a reference implementation. It does not make timing comparisons fair; it checks observable behavior.

**Design (applied):** Write the smallest operation sequence that reveals a stale-tail bug. State the expected result before running it.

```{index} memory locality; reference type; allocation
```



```{index} Memory and Locality Qualify the Recommendation
```

## Memory and Locality Qualify the Recommendation



For `int` elements, the backing array places the integer values together. For reference-type elements, the reference slots are contiguous but their target objects need not be. Sequential array access often benefits from memory locality. A linked traversal follows separately allocated node objects, which may be scattered in memory.

Linked lists also pay for a node object and link field per item. Dynamic arrays pay for spare capacity and occasional replacement arrays. Neither representation has universally smaller memory usage: the element type, spare capacity, object layout, and workload matter.

Begin with a dynamic array such as `List<T>` for ordinary indexed application sequences. Justify a linked structure when its operations and API offer a concrete benefit, such as repeated front removal or insertion at already known positions. Do not replace every `List<T>` just because some linked updates have constant cost.

**Decision memo (challenge):** Recommend a representation for a dispatch application. Give two frequent operations, one worst-case risk, a memory tradeoff, and a measurement that could change your recommendation.

```{index} summary
```



```{index} Summary
```

## Summary



Arrays and linked lists both represent sequences, but they optimize different operations. A strong data-structure choice starts with the workload: what the program does most often, what must be fast, and what tradeoffs are acceptable.


```{rubric} Footnotes
```


[^1403_comparison_lab-1]: Later chapters revisit these same tradeoffs in stacks, queues, trees, hash tables, and graphs.

title: Stacks & Queues

# Stacks & Queues This chapter covers stacks, queues, deques, restricted-access ADTs, array-based implementations, linked implementations, and applications such as undo, scheduling, buffering, backtracking, and breadth-first processing. The sidebar title focuses on the two central access rules: last-in-first-out and first-in-first-out. - **Stack**: A stack uses last-in, first-out behavior for undo, nested processing, and backtracking. - **Queue**: A queue uses first-in, first-out behavior for service lines and scheduled work. - **Deque**: A deque supports insertion and removal at both ends, making it a flexible boundary structure. - **Implementation choice**: Array-based and linked implementations can provide the same ADT operations with different costs. - **Application fit**: Restricted-access structures are useful when the rule for who comes next is part of the problem. Stacks, queues, and deques show that a data structure is not only storage. It is also a policy for how a program is allowed to use that storage.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: G0bD3Af1DRc :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[C# Data Structures - Arrays, Lists, Dictionaries, HashSets, Stacks, Queues](https://youtube.com/watch?v=G0bD3Af1DRc)* by Mark Inman. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Specify stack, queue, and deque access rules and failure behavior. 2. Trace count, capacity, stack top, and ring-buffer wraparound. 3. overview:
# Stacks & Queues

This chapter covers stacks, queues, deques, restricted-access ADTs, array-based implementations, linked implementations, and applications such as undo, scheduling, buffering, backtracking, and breadth-first processing. The sidebar title focuses on the two central access rules: last-in-first-out and first-in-first-out.

- **Stack**: A stack uses last-in, first-out behavior for undo, nested processing, and backtracking.
- **Queue**: A queue uses first-in, first-out behavior for service lines and scheduled work.
- **Deque**: A deque supports insertion and removal at both ends, making it a flexible boundary structure.
- **Implementation choice**: Array-based and linked implementations can provide the same ADT operations with different costs.
- **Application fit**: Restricted-access structures are useful when the rule for who comes next is part of the problem.

Stacks, queues, and deques show that a data structure is not only storage. It is also a policy for how a program is allowed to use that storage.

# Trees - **Hierarchy**: Trees represent parent-child relationships with one root and no cycles. - **Recursive structure**: Count nodes, leaves, and height by combining child-subtree results. - **Traversal**: Trace depth-first and level-order visits and choose an order for a task. - **Binary search tree**: Maintain a unique-key ordering invariant during search, insertion, and removal. - **Shape and cost**: Explain how height controls path operations and how pruning supports range reports. A service desk's active ticket IDs provide an ordered-set example. Department hierarchies show how general trees differ from binary search trees.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: J2fol8eWo64 :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[Data Structures - Full Course for Beginners](https://youtube.com/watch?v=J2fol8eWo64)* by Tech With Tim. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Explain base cases, smaller recursive calls, and suspended call frames. 2. Distinguish a general tree, a binary tree, and a binary search tree. 3. Trace preorder, inorder, postorder, and level-order traversal. 4. Compute node count, leaf count, and height using explicit base cases. 5. overview:
# Trees

- **Hierarchy**: Trees represent parent-child relationships with one root and no cycles.
- **Recursive structure**: Count nodes, leaves, and height by combining child-subtree results.
- **Traversal**: Trace depth-first and level-order visits and choose an order for a task.
- **Binary search tree**: Maintain a unique-key ordering invariant during search, insertion, and removal.
- **Shape and cost**: Explain how height controls path operations and how pruning supports range reports.

A service desk's active ticket IDs provide an ordered-set example. Department hierarchies show how general trees differ from binary search trees.

# Graphs and Traversal This chapter develops contracts, runnable implementations, and the tradeoffs needed to choose a structure or algorithm for a business information system. Complete the three lessons and the connected practice before choosing optional extensions. - **Traversal verification**: Breadth-first and depth-first search explore graph structure in different orders. - **Reachability**: A question about whether one state, vertex, or item can be reached from another. Traversal verification connects these foundations to later path assumptions, string matching, computational limits, pruning, approximation and final algorithm selection.

Learning Objectives

- Explain the chapter contracts and boundary cases. - Trace the implementation and justify its operation costs. - Select and test a suitable approach for a stated workload. - Explain BFS discovery and layer invariants and reconstruct valid minimum-hop paths. - Trace DFS entry/exit with explicit frames and enforce undirected-component preconditions.

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`20.1. Graph Vocabulary and Models <2001_graph_vocabulary>` - {doc}`20.2. Adjacency Representations <2002_adjacency_representations>` - {doc}`20.3. Breadth-First Search and Paths <2003_graph_traversal>` - {doc}`20.4. Depth-First Search and Components <2004_depth_first_components>` {doc}`Assignments `

Glossary

| Term | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Vertex | An explicitly represented entity. | | Edge | A connection with a direction and optional weight contract. | | BFS | Queue-based discovery in distance layers. | | DFS | Explore a branch before returning to other neighbors. | | Predecessor | The earlier vertex stored at discovery for route recovery. | | Component | A maximal connected group in an undirected graph. | | Breadth-first search | A graph traversal that explores vertices in layers using a queue. | | Depth-first search | A graph traversal that explores along one path before backtracking. | | Reachability | Whether a target vertex or state can be reached from a starting point. | | Traversal order | The order in which an algorithm visits vertices or states. | | Shortest path | A path with minimum number of edges or minimum total cost. | | Discovery | First reaching and marking a vertex before adding it to a worklist. | | DFS frame | A vertex and suspended next-neighbor position on the active exploration stack. |

Teaching Materials

The runnable notebooks and assignments are ready for practice. Matching slides and recorded walkthroughs for the revised sequence remain in preparation.

# Analysis This chapter covers algorithm correctness, specifications, preconditions, postconditions, loop invariants, operation counting, Big-O/Big-Theta notation, space growth, and recurrence relations. The sidebar title **Analysis** names the skill: reasoning about whether an algorithm works and how its cost grows. - **Correctness**: A claim that an algorithm satisfies its specification for every valid input. - **Complexity**: A description of how time or memory use grows as input size grows. - **Big-O**: An upper-bound growth description that ignores constant factors and lower-order terms. - **Invariant**: A fact that remains true before and after each loop iteration. - **Recurrence**: An equation that describes the cost of a recursive algorithm in terms of smaller inputs. Algorithm analysis asks two questions: does the procedure always produce the required result, and how do its time and memory needs grow as the input grows?

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: IcDcNp8gZ7U :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[Data Structures and Algorithms In C#: Big-O Notation](https://youtube.com/watch?v=IcDcNp8gZ7U)* by Teddy Smith. > > This video is a quick supplement for the growth-rate ideas in this chapter. The chapter develops the notation, correctness language, and recurrence reasoning in the book's sequence.

Learning Objectives

1. Define input sizes and a cost model; derive exact counts for sequential, rectangular, triangular, and halving loops. 2. Distinguish upper, lower, and tight bounds and best, worst, expected, and amortized costs. 3. State precise contracts and use initialization, maintenance, exit reasoning, and decreasing variants to establish total correctness. 4. Choose boundary tests and counterexamples that challenge an implementation. 5. Derive recurrences with base cases and rounding; separate modeled work, total calls, stack depth, and other auxiliary storage.

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`21.1. Big-O and Complexity <2101_big_o>` - {doc}`21.2. Correctness and Invariants <2102_correctness>` - {doc}`21.3. Recurrences and Recursive Cost <2103_recurrences>`

Glossary

| # | Term | Explanation | |---:|---|---| | 1 | Input size | A measure of how large the input is, usually written as `n`. | | 2 | Growth rate | A description of how work or memory changes as input size increases. | | 3 | Big-O | An asymptotic upper bound on growth. | | 4 | Big-Theta | An asymptotically tight growth description. | | 5 | Constant time | A cost that does not grow with input size. | | 6 | Linear time | A cost that grows proportionally with input size. | | 7 | Logarithmic time | A cost that grows by repeatedly reducing the problem size by a factor. | | 8 | Precondition | A condition that must be true before an algorithm runs. | | 9 | Postcondition | A condition that should be true after an algorithm finishes. | | 10 | Loop invariant | A fact that is true before and after every loop iteration. | | 11 | Recurrence relation | An equation that defines a recursive algorithm cost using smaller inputs. | | 12 | Big-Omega | An asymptotic lower bound. | | 13 | Cost model | The operations and assumptions used to count work. | | 14 | Auxiliary space | Storage used in addition to the input, under a stated output convention. | | 15 | Variant | A nonnegative integer measure that strictly decreases on continuing loop iterations. | | 16 | Partial correctness | The postcondition holds if execution terminates on a valid input. | | 17 | Total correctness | Partial correctness plus guaranteed termination. | | 18 | Worst-case cost | Maximum cost over valid inputs of a given size. | | 19 | Expected cost | A cost average under a stated probability model. | | 20 | Amortized cost | Cost per operation averaged over an operation sequence. | | 21 | Recursion depth | Maximum simultaneously active calls, under a stated counting convention. |

# Recursion This chapter covers recursive methods, base cases, recursive cases, progress measures, call-stack tracing, divide-and-conquer design, binary search as a halving example, merge, and merge sort. The sidebar title **Recursion** names the core mechanism; divide-and-conquer is the main algorithm-design pattern built from it. - **Base case**: The condition that stops recursion with a direct answer. - **Recursive case**: The part of the method that calls itself on a smaller input. - **Progress measure**: A quantity that moves toward the base case on every recursive call. - **Call stack**: The runtime structure that tracks active method calls and their local variables. - **Divide-and-conquer**: A design pattern that divides a problem, solves subproblems, and combines results. Recursion is ordinary method calls plus the call stack. Divide-and-conquer uses that mechanism to split a problem, solve smaller parts, and combine the answers. This chapter is optional for the College of Business pathway. Its foundations are taught in Part V; review {doc}`recursive calls in Chapter 17 <../17_trees/1701_tree_structure>` before the advanced work here.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: 8hly31xKli0 :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[Algorithms and Data Structures Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners](https://youtube.com/watch?v=8hly31xKli0)* by freeCodeCamp.org. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

1. State recursive input domains, base cases, helper contracts, and well-founded progress measures. 2. Trace separate call frames and returned results, including arithmetic and stack limits. 3. Prove range splits preserve all items and distinguish one-child search from two-child division. 4. Implement stable merge and merge sort with explicit tie and copy policies. 5. Verify order, occurrence preservation, input identity, and stable record order across boundary cases. 6. Relate actual comparisons, writes, calls, and active depth to time and auxiliary-space bounds.

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`22.1. Recursive Contracts and Divide-and-Conquer <2201_recursion>` - {doc}`22.2. Stable Merge Sort and Verification <2203_merge_sort_lab>`

Glossary

| # | Term | Explanation | |---:|---|---| | 1 | Recursion | A technique where a method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller input. | | 2 | Base case | A directly solved case that stops recursive calls. | | 3 | Recursive case | The branch that makes one or more recursive calls. | | 4 | Progress measure | A value, such as `n` or a range length, that gets closer to the base case with each call. | | 5 | Call stack | The runtime stack of active method calls. | | 6 | Stack frame | One active method call and its local state on the call stack. | | 7 | Divide-and-conquer | An algorithm design pattern that splits a problem into subproblems, solves them, and combines the answers. | | 8 | Subproblem | A smaller version of the original problem. | | 9 | Combine step | The step that merges subproblem results into a final answer. | | 10 | Merge | The process of combining two sorted sequences into one sorted sequence. | | 11 | Merge sort | A divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that recursively sorts halves and merges them. | | 12 | Half-open range | A range [start,end) including start but excluding end. | | 13 | Helper contract | The promise made by a recursive subproblem method. | | 14 | Inductive reasoning | A direct base result plus a correct combination of smaller correct results. | | 15 | Stable sort | A sort preserving arrival order among equal comparison keys. | | 16 | Occurrence preservation | Keeping every input item with its original multiplicity. | | 17 | Shared merge buffer | A reusable temporary array used by successive merges. | | 18 | Shallow array copy | A new array whose element references or values are copied without cloning referenced objects. | | 19 | Peak active frames | Maximum calls simultaneously retained on the stack, including the base frame here. |

| 15 | Stable sort | A sort preserving arrival order among equal comparison keys. |
| 16 | Occurrence preservation | Keeping every input item with its original multiplicity. |
| 17 | Shared merge buffer | A reusable temporary array used by successive merges. |
| 18 | Shallow array copy | A new array whose element references or values are copied without cloning referenced objects. |
| 19 | Peak active frames | Maximum calls simultaneously retained on the stack, including the base frame here. |

# Advanced Searching and Sorting This chapter covers linear search, binary search, search preconditions, swap operations, elementary sorting algorithms, comparison counts, correctness tests, and when to use library sorting. The sidebar title **Search & Sort** keeps the two algorithm families visible without crowding the navigation. - **Linear search**: Checks items one by one until the target is found or the input ends. - **Binary search**: Uses sorted order to discard half of the remaining search range at each step. - **Elementary sort**: A simple sorting algorithm, such as selection sort, insertion sort, or bubble sort, that is easy to trace but usually quadratic. - **Comparison count**: A useful operation count for algorithms that decide order by comparing values. - **Data condition**: Some algorithms require data to be sorted or structured before they are valid. Searching locates data. Sorting puts data into an order that makes later work easier, including faster searching. This chapter is optional for the College of Business pathway. Its foundations are taught in Part IV; review {doc}`sequence search and library sorting in Chapter 16 <../16_searching_sorting/1601_searching>` before the advanced work here.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: 8hly31xKli0 :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[Algorithms and Data Structures Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners](https://youtube.com/watch?v=8hly31xKli0)* by freeCodeCamp.org. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

1. Specify first, any, and all-match search contracts with compatible equality and ordering policies. 2. Trace half-open binary search and derive lower/upper bounds for duplicate groups and insertion positions. 3. Explain selection, insertion, and optimized bubble sorts using invariants and occurrence preservation. 4. Derive exact selection comparisons and relate insertion shifts and adjacent swaps to inversions. 5. Verify stable record order, sorted permutations, and explicit mutation/library return policies. 6. Compare complete workloads including preparation, queries, input order, updates, and storage.

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`23.1. Searching <2301_searching>` - {doc}`23.2. Sorting <2302_sorting>` - {doc}`23.3. Comparing Complete Search and Sort Workloads <2303_comparison_lab>` - {doc}`23.4. Shell Sort and Gap Families (Supporting reading) <2304_advanced_sorts>` - {doc}`23.5. Quicksort and Partitioning (Supporting reading) <2305_quicksort>`

Glossary

| # | Term | Explanation | |---:|---|---| | 1 | Search | The task of finding whether and where a value appears. | | 2 | Linear search | A search algorithm that checks items sequentially. | | 3 | Binary search | A search algorithm for sorted data that repeatedly halves the remaining search range. | | 4 | Sorted order | An arrangement where values follow a chosen ordering rule. | | 5 | Comparison | A test that decides how two values relate in an order. | | 6 | Swap | An operation that exchanges values at two positions. | | 7 | Selection sort | A sorting algorithm that repeatedly selects the smallest remaining value and moves it into place. | | 8 | Insertion sort | A sorting algorithm that grows a sorted prefix by inserting each new item into its correct position. | | 9 | Bubble sort | A sorting algorithm that repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order values. | | 10 | Stable sort | A sort that preserves the relative order of items with equal comparison keys. | | 11 | In-place sort | A sort that uses only small extra storage beyond the input array. | | 12 | Any-match search | Returns a matching index without guaranteeing the first duplicate. | | 13 | Lower bound | First sorted position with a key at least the target, or the length. | | 14 | Upper bound | First sorted position with a key greater than the target, or the length. | | 15 | Probe | One selected equality/comparer call in a search. | | 16 | Inversion | A pair of positions whose earlier key is greater than the later key. | | 17 | Shift | An insertion-sort move of a greater predecessor one position right. | | 18 | Sorted permutation | Ordered output containing every input occurrence with the same multiplicity. | | 19 | Preparation cost | Work to construct a search representation before answering queries. | | 20 | Sorted snapshot | An ordered view that may need rebuilding or maintenance after updates. |

Slides

# Greedy Algorithms This chapter covers greedy choice rules, feasibility, invariants, counterexamples, exchange arguments, minimum spanning trees, Kruskal's algorithm, shortest paths, and Dijkstra's algorithm. The sidebar title **Greedy Algorithms** names the design strategy; graph optimization provides the main application setting. - **Greedy choice**: A locally best option selected without revisiting earlier choices. - **Feasible solution**: A partial or complete solution that satisfies the problem constraints. - **Invariant**: A property that remains true after each greedy step. - **Minimum spanning tree**: A lowest-cost set of edges that connects every vertex in an undirected weighted graph without cycles. - **Shortest path**: A lowest-cost route from a source vertex to another vertex under specific edge-weight assumptions. Greedy algorithms are powerful when the local rule matches the global goal. This chapter studies how to recognize when that is true and when it is a trap.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: 09_LlHjoEiY :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[Graph Theory Algorithms](https://youtube.com/watch?v=09_LlHjoEiY)* by freeCodeCamp.org. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Specify an optimization objective and distinguish feasibility from optimality. 2. Prove maximum-count interval scheduling with an exchange argument and test changed objectives with counterexamples. 3. Trace Kruskal’s union-find invariant and report a minimum spanning forest for disconnected inputs. 4. Explain Dijkstra’s settling argument, reject negative arcs, and skip stale queue entries. 5. Reconstruct reachable paths, represent unreachable vertices explicitly, and verify costs without integer overflow. 6. Choose between network cost and source-to-destination distance using independent small-instance checks.

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`24.1. Greedy Choices and Exchange Reasoning <2401_greedy_choice>` - {doc}`24.2. Minimum Spanning Forests and Kruskal <2402_spanning_trees_shortest_paths>` - {doc}`24.3. Shortest Paths and Dijkstra <2404_shortest_paths>`

Glossary

| # | Term | Explanation | |---:|---|---| | 1 | Greedy algorithm | An algorithm that builds a solution by repeatedly choosing the locally best available option. | | 2 | Greedy choice | The local decision made at one step of a greedy algorithm. | | 3 | Feasible solution | A solution, or partial solution, that does not violate the problem constraints. | | 4 | Objective function | The quantity an optimization algorithm tries to minimize or maximize. | | 5 | Invariant | A fact that remains true after each step of an algorithm. | | 6 | Exchange argument | A proof technique that shows an optimal solution can be adjusted to include the greedy choice. | | 7 | Minimum spanning tree | A tree that connects all vertices in an undirected weighted graph with minimum total edge weight. | | 8 | Kruskal algorithm | A greedy minimum-spanning-tree algorithm that adds safe edges in increasing weight order. | | 9 | Shortest path | A path with minimum total edge weight between vertices. | | 10 | Dijkstra algorithm | A greedy shortest-path algorithm for graphs with nonnegative edge weights. | | 11 | Minimum spanning forest | A minimum-cost tree in each connected component, including isolated vertices. | | 12 | Union-find | A component representation supporting root lookup and component merging. | | 13 | Relaxation | Improving a tentative distance through an edge from a reached vertex. | | 14 | Stale queue entry | An older priority that no longer equals the vertex’s best known distance. |

Slides

Slides for this chapter will be added after the notebook content stabilizes.

# Dynamic Programming This chapter covers overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, memoization, tabulation, small dynamic-programming tables, backtracking, search spaces, undo steps, and pruning. The sidebar title **Dynamic Programming** names the main optimization technique; backtracking is included as the paired strategy for systematic search. - **Overlapping subproblems**: The same smaller problem appears repeatedly. - **Optimal substructure**: A larger solution can be built from smaller optimal solutions. - **Memoization**: A top-down technique that stores recursive results for reuse. - **Tabulation**: A bottom-up technique that fills a table from small cases to large cases. - **Backtracking**: A search pattern that makes a choice, explores it, then undoes the choice. Dynamic programming controls repeated work. Backtracking controls large choice spaces by exploring, undoing, and pruning.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: oBt53YbR9Kk :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[Dynamic Programming - Learn to Solve Algorithmic Problems & Coding Challenges](https://youtube.com/watch?v=oBt53YbR9Kk)* by freeCodeCamp.org. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Define a complete state, recurrence, base cases, and dependency order. 2. Compare naive recursion, memoization, tabulation, and rolling state using the same input and counting policy. 3. Compute minimum reusable-pack counts, represent unreachable quantities, and reconstruct a valid optimal plan. 4. Search one-use signed records with position-aware states, safe suffix bounds, and failed-state memoization. 5. Preserve shared-state invariants through undo and independent result snapshots. 6. Verify solutions against small independent references and explain output costs and resource limits.

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`25.1. Memoization, Tabulation, and Repeated Work <2501_memoization_tabulation>` - {doc}`25.2. Optimization States and Reconstructed Solutions <2504_optimization_models>` - {doc}`25.3. Backtracking, Pruning, and Search States <2502_backtracking>`

Glossary

| # | Term | Explanation | |---:|---|---| | 1 | Dynamic programming | A technique that solves repeated subproblems once and reuses their answers. | | 2 | Overlapping subproblems | A property where the same smaller problems occur multiple times inside a larger problem. | | 3 | Optimal substructure | A property where an optimal solution can be built from optimal solutions to smaller problems. | | 4 | Memoization | Top-down dynamic programming that caches recursive results. | | 5 | Tabulation | Bottom-up dynamic programming that fills a table in dependency order. | | 6 | State | The information that identifies one subproblem. | | 7 | Transition | A rule that computes one state from smaller or earlier states. | | 8 | Backtracking | A search technique that makes a choice, explores recursively, then undoes the choice. | | 9 | Choice | One option selected at a search step. | | 10 | Pruning | Skipping a search branch because it cannot lead to a valid or better solution. | | 11 | Search tree | The implicit tree of choices explored by a recursive search. | | 12 | Witness | A concrete solution whose constraints and objective can be checked. | | 13 | Suffix bound | A proven lower or upper limit on what unprocessed positions can sum to. | | 14 | Pseudo-polynomial time | Time bounded by numeric values such as the target, rather than just their encoded length. | | 15 | Unknown result | A search stopped by a resource limit before establishing feasibility or infeasibility. |

# Advanced Algorithms This chapter develops direct string matching, reusable prefix information, computational growth, and the difference between exact answers and heuristic results. Connect each method to its result contract: which matches count, what work can be reused, and what evidence supports a claimed answer. - **String matching**: Searching for a pattern inside a larger text. - **Prefix reuse**: Retaining a proven matching suffix instead of restarting every comparison. - **Computational limit**: A point where exact brute-force computation grows too quickly to be practical. - **Approximation**: A method with a proved quality bound relative to the optimum under stated assumptions. The goal is not to memorize every advanced algorithm, but to recognize how problem structure shapes what efficient computation can do. This chapter is optional for the College of Business pathway. Its foundations are taught in Part V; review {doc}`graph traversal in Chapter 20 <../20_graphs/2003_graph_traversal>` before the advanced work here.

Chapter Video

```{eval-rst} .. youtube:: 09_LlHjoEiY :width: 560 :height: 315 ``` > *[Graph Theory Algorithms](https://youtube.com/watch?v=09_LlHjoEiY)* by freeCodeCamp.org. > > This video remains hosted on YouTube and is the property of its original creator or rightsholder; it is embedded here via YouTube's official player for educational reference only. This retained video reviews the graph foundations used in the service-network assignments. The core reading sequence below focuses on strings and computational limits.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Implement direct and prepared-prefix matching under explicit ordinal, overlap, and empty-pattern contracts. 2. Justify prefix fallback and linear comparison bounds, including preparation and output costs. 3. Validate exact and heuristic coverage witnesses and distinguish feasibility, optimality, and proved approximation guarantees. 4. Compare complete workloads and exact growth models without confusing measurements with general lower-bound proofs.

Chapter Flow

- {doc}`26.1. Direct String Matching and Result Contracts <2602_shortest_paths_strings>` - {doc}`26.2. Prefix Reuse and KMP <2604_prefix_matching>` - {doc}`26.3. Algorithms and Computational Limits <2603_limits_project>` For traversal verification, return to {doc}`Chapter 20 <../20_graphs/2004_depth_first_components>`; for hop-versus-cost objectives, review {doc}`Chapter 24 <../24_greedy_graph_optimization/2404_shortest_paths>`.

Glossary

| # | Term | Explanation | |---:|---|---| | 1 | String matching | Finding whether and where a pattern occurs in a text. | | 2 | Pattern | The string or structure being searched for. | | 3 | Text | The larger string being searched. | | 4 | Prefix table | A table that records reusable information about matching prefixes in a pattern. | | 5 | Intractable problem | A problem considered computationally difficult in a stated model; one slow implementation alone does not prove this classification. | | 6 | Approximation | An algorithm with a proved objective bound relative to the optimum under stated assumptions. | | 7 | Limit | A constraint, such as time or memory, that shapes algorithm choice. | | 8 | Border | A proper pattern prefix that is also a suffix of the matched segment. | | 9 | Ordinal match | Equality of UTF-16 code units without culture rules, case folding, or normalization. | | 10 | Heuristic | A practical method used without an optimality or approximation guarantee established here. |

Slides

Slides for this chapter will be added after the notebook content stabilizes.

| 2 | Pattern | The string or structure being searched for. |
| 3 | Text | The larger string being searched. |
| 4 | Prefix table | A table that records reusable information about matching prefixes in a pattern. |
| 5 | Intractable problem | A problem considered computationally difficult in a stated model; one slow implementation alone does not prove this classification. |
| 6 | Approximation | An algorithm with a proved objective bound relative to the optimum under stated assumptions. |
| 7 | Limit | A constraint, such as time or memory, that shapes algorithm choice. |

| 8 | Border | A proper pattern prefix that is also a suffix of the matched segment. |
| 9 | Ordinal match | Equality of UTF-16 code units without culture rules, case folding, or normalization. |
| 10 | Heuristic | A practical method used without an optimality or approximation guarantee established here. |
